questions.text: Blocks as one story: the level of the block decides everything

steps.bridge: Two failures: a tired gate and a broken wire. Before the gate, though, the pacemaker itself can fail. Start at the top.

lesson.text:
Here is the sentence this whole section hangs on. First-degree block, Mobitz one, Mobitz two and complete block are not four diseases to memorise. They are two, and you already know both, because you have met the two kinds of cell.

Go back to the relay. The AV node is built from calcium cells. They conduct slowly and stay refractory for a while even after they have repolarised, so a calcium cell that is pushed does not fail suddenly. It tires. Each impulse that arrives a little too soon crosses a little more slowly. That was decremental conduction. Below the node, the bundle of His, the bundle branches and the Purkinje fibres are sodium cells. Sodium gates slam open or stay shut. A sodium cell conducts at full speed or not at all.

So conduction can fail in only two ways: a tired gate, or a broken wire. Watch each one draw its strip.

The tired gate first. The first P wave reaches a rested node and crosses with a normal PR. The second arrives before the node has fully recovered, so it crosses more slowly and the PR is longer. The PR stretches, beat after beat, until one P wave finds the node completely refractory and does not cross. No QRS follows it. That missed beat is the node's rest, so the next P crosses with the shortest PR of the cycle, and the sequence begins again. This is Mobitz one, the Wenckebach pattern. First-degree block is the same tired node on a milder day: every P crosses, each one slowly.

Three details of Wenckebach are asked as statements, and each falls out of the mechanism. The longest PR is the one just before the dropped beat, and the shortest is the one just after it. The pause is shorter than two P to P intervals, because the beat that ends it conducts quickly. And the odd one: before the pause, the R to R intervals get shorter, not longer. The PR grows with every beat, but it grows by a smaller amount each time, so the QRS complexes crowd together. NEET's favourite wrong statement here is that the R to R interval lengthens before the dropped beat.

Now the broken wire. Nothing tires here. Every beat that conducts does so at full speed, so the PR is the same before the dropped beat and after it. Then, with no warning, a P wave that arrives exactly on time is followed by nothing. That is Mobitz two. Because the fault lies in the bundles, the QRS is often wide. And it is dangerous, because the next stage is no conduction at all, with only a slow ventricular pacemaker left.

[[Mobitz one is a tired calcium node: the PR lengthens, then a beat drops. Mobitz two is a broken sodium wire below the node: the PR is constant, then a beat drops without warning.]]

Now bring in the autonomic hands. The vagus and the sympathetic nerves grip the node firmly and hardly reach the wiring below it. That gives three tests. Atropine and exercise speed the node, so a nodal block improves. They cannot mend a wire, but they do speed the sinus rate, so more impulses reach a wire that can pass only so many, and a block below the node gets worse. Carotid massage does the reverse on both. It slows the node, so a nodal block worsens. And by slowing the sinus rate it gives the diseased wire longer to recover, so a block below the node may improve.

{{**The level decides**
Feature | Node (calcium) | Below the node (sodium)
Pattern | first degree, Mobitz I | Mobitz II
PR | lengthens | constant
QRS | usually narrow | often wide
Atropine, exercise | improve | worsen or no change
Carotid massage | worsens | may improve
Course | benign | progresses; pace}}

One caution: a Wenckebach pattern with a wide QRS can occasionally come from below the node, but Mobitz two, properly defined, is always below it.

[[Atropine and exercise improve a nodal block and worsen a block below the node. Carotid massage does the opposite. In a block, find the level first.]]

But an impulse has to be made before it can be blocked, so begin one step higher, at the pacemaker.
lesson.cap: Mobitz I: PR lengthens until a beat drops (node, usually benign). Mobitz II: PR fixed, sudden drop, often wide QRS (below the node, pace).

steps.bridge: The pacemaker can be slow, or its impulse can fail to get out. Now follow the impulse to the gate and name each block properly.

lesson.text:
Before the gate, the pacemaker. Bradycardia is a rate under sixty, and the first question is simply whether the sinus node is still in charge.

In sinus bradycardia it is. The node fires slowly and nothing else is wrong, so every QRS has a normal upright P in front of it and a normal PR. Remember the pacemaker potential: the rate is set by the slope of phase four, and the vagus flattens that slope. So sleep and athletic training do it, drugs do it, and the card lists the pathological causes: hypoxia, infarction, raised intracranial pressure and hypothyroidism. The infarct is usually inferior, because the right coronary artery feeds the node and the inferior wall sets off a vagal reflex.

Now suppose the sinus node fails. You met the back-up pacemakers in the relay: the AV junction waits at forty to sixty a minute, silenced only because the sinus node is faster. When the sinus rate falls below it, the junction takes over. The impulse runs down the normal wiring, so the QRS is narrow. And it runs backwards, up into the atria, away from the camera of lead two. Away from a camera is a downward wave. So the P is inverted in lead two, three and aVF, and depending on timing it sits just before the QRS, hides inside it, or follows it.

[[A normal upright P before every QRS is sinus bradycardia. An inverted, absent or late P with a narrow QRS is a junctional rhythm: the back-up pacemaker has taken over.]]

The card's causes of a junctional rhythm are hyperkalaemia, severe sinus bradycardia and sino-atrial exit block. That last one is asked, and it is the gate and the wire all over again, at the mouth of the sinus node. The node fires on time, but the impulse fails to get out into the atrium. You cannot see the node fire. You only see a missing P wave, so you do arithmetic on the P to P intervals. In type two exit block the rhythm is constant and then one whole cycle is missing: the pause is an exact multiple of the P to P interval, usually double. In type one, the Wenckebach form, the P to P intervals shorten and then comes a pause of less than two cycles, the same crowding you have just learned. A sinus pause or arrest has no fixed relation to the cycle, because the node itself stopped.

NEET's wrong option for a constant rhythm with a pause of exactly two cycles is sinus arrest. It is exit block, type two.

So that is failure at the top. Now the impulse has left the atrium and stands at the gate.
lesson.cap: SA exit block: the pause is an exact multiple of the P-P interval. Sinus arrest: the pause bears no relation to it.

steps.bridge: When no P wave crosses at all, atria and ventricles each keep their own time. That is complete block.

lesson.text:
You have the two failures. This card puts the official names and numbers on them, and it is the most heavily asked card of the section, so take the stems as you go.

First degree. Every P conducts, one to one, but slowly: a PR longer than zero point two zero seconds, which is one large square. Nothing is actually blocked. It is a slow node, from vagal tone, drugs, an inferior infarct or myocarditis, and it usually needs nothing. One item gave an asymptomatic patient with first-degree block, and only thirty-nine per cent chose to discharge him. Do not admit a long PR.

Second degree means some P waves cross and some do not. Mobitz one: progressive PR lengthening, then a dropped QRS. NEET twenty twenty-five asked exactly that. Mobitz two: a fixed PR, then a dropped QRS. Marrow asked it backwards: which feature is not seen in type one block? Worsening with atropine.

Now the difficulty. Suppose every second P is dropped, two P waves for each QRS. That is two to one block. There are never two conducted beats in a row, so you cannot say whether the PR was lengthening, and the strip alone cannot be called Mobitz one or Mobitz two. The card says so in its last line. You go back to the level, and you use four clues. The width of the QRS: narrow suggests the node, wide suggests the bundles. The PR of the beats that do conduct: a long PR suggests the node is the tired part. The company it keeps: a sleeping athlete or an inferior infarct against an anterior infarct or an elderly patient with syncope. And the response to atropine or exercise, or simply a longer strip that catches a stretch of three to two conduction and shows the PR lengthening.

[[Two to one block cannot be classified from the PR. A narrow QRS in a vagal setting means the node. A wide QRS or an anterior infarct means below the node.]]

The grand test stem was a sleeping athlete with two to one block and a narrow QRS, and only forty-two per cent placed it in the AV node. The wrong options were the His bundle and the bundle branches.

One step worse is high-grade or advanced block: two or more P waves in a row fail to conduct, but some still do, so there is still a relationship. And when none conducts at all, it is complete heart block, which has its own lesson next.

Two more things from the bank. First, a wrong key. One item shows second-degree block after an anterior infarct and keys it as Mobitz one, benign, give atropine. The anterior descending artery feeds the wiring below the node, so that block is in the His-Purkinje system and needs a pacing wire. On the day choose the option that says so. Second, a mimic. A premature atrial beat that comes too early to conduct also gives a P wave with no QRS after it. But that P is early, and it usually sits on the T wave of the beat before and deforms it. In Mobitz two the dropped P is exactly on time.

{{**AV blocks**
First degree | PR > 0.20 s, every P conducts
Mobitz I | PR lengthens, then a drop
Mobitz II | PR constant, then a drop
2:1 | unclassifiable by PR; use QRS width and setting
High-grade | 2 or more P in a row not conducted
Complete | no relationship}}

[[First-degree block is a PR over zero point two zero seconds with every P conducted, and it is sent home. High-grade block is two or more consecutive P waves not conducted.]]

Now let the gate close altogether.
lesson.cap: First degree: PR > 0.20 s, all conducted. 2:1: type by QRS width and response, not PR. High-grade: ≥ 2 consecutive P waves blocked.

steps.bridge: The escape rhythm told you the level. The coronary artery tells you the same thing in an infarct.

lesson.text:
In complete heart block no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles. So picture two clocks. The sinus node drives the atria at its own rate, say eighty. Below the block, a back-up pacemaker drives the ventricles at its own slower rate. Each clock is regular. Neither knows about the other.

On the strip the P waves march through at even spacing. The QRS complexes march through at their own even, slower spacing. And the PR changes with every beat, at random, because there is no real PR. Regular P waves, regular QRS complexes, no relationship, and more P waves than QRS complexes.

That last phrase protects you from a trap in the wording. AV dissociation only means the atria and ventricles are beating independently. Complete block is one cause of it. The other is a lower pacemaker that has simply become faster than the sinus node, as in ventricular tachycardia or an accelerated junctional rhythm. In those the ventricular rate is the faster one, and conduction may be perfectly healthy. So when the atria are faster and nothing gets through, it is block. When the ventricles are faster, it is dissociation without block.

[[Complete heart block: regular P waves, regular slower QRS complexes, no relationship between them. AV dissociation with the ventricles faster than the atria is not block.]]

Now the level, the question of this section. In complete block you read it from the escape rhythm, because the escape pacemaker sits just below the block. If the node is blocked, the junction escapes. It fires at forty to sixty a minute, it uses the normal wiring, so the QRS is narrow, it is reliable, and it still listens to atropine a little. That is the block of an inferior infarct and of congenital complete block, in which antibodies of the anti-Ro type cross from the mother and scar the fetal node. If the wiring below the node is blocked, only the ventricle is left. It fires at twenty to forty, the impulse crawls from muscle cell to muscle cell, so the QRS is wide, and it is unreliable: it can stop, and then the patient faints or dies. That is the block of an anterior infarct, of age-related fibrosis of the conducting system, which carries the names Lenegre and Lev, and of a catheter-implanted aortic valve, which presses on the bundle of His just beneath it.

{{**Complete block: the escape gives the level**
 | Junctional escape | Ventricular escape
QRS | narrow | wide
Rate | 40–60 | 20–40
Level | AV node | His–Purkinje
Atropine | some response | none
Reliability | fair | poor: asystole risk}}

The bedside signs are the two clocks again. Now and then the atrium contracts when the ventricle is already contracting and the tricuspid valve is shut. The blood can only go backwards, up the neck: a cannon a wave, appearing irregularly. And the first heart sound varies in loudness from beat to beat, because the valve leaflets are caught in a different position each time. Contrast atrial fibrillation, where there is no atrial contraction at all, so there is no a wave. That contrast has been asked.

The causes sort by the same two levels and are mostly reversible ones to look for: degenerative fibrosis, an infarct, the nodal drugs, hyperkalaemia, myocarditis, sarcoidosis and Lyme disease, hypothermia, and cardiac surgery. One is a favourite stem. A patient with endocarditis of the aortic valve whose PR starts to lengthen has an abscess of the aortic root, burrowing into the conducting tissue beside it.

Treatment is to supply the missing rate: pads for transcutaneous pacing at once, then a transvenous wire, with isoprenaline or adrenaline as a bridge. The doses and the algorithm come in the Rhythm packet.

[[The escape rhythm gives the level. Narrow at forty to sixty is junctional, under a blocked node. Wide at twenty to forty is ventricular, under blocked wiring, and it is unreliable.]]

Next, the place you will meet this most often: the infarct.
lesson.cap: Complete block: P and QRS on separate clocks. Narrow escape 40–60 = block in the node; wide escape 20–40 = block below it.

steps.bridge: The infarct showed atropine working at one level and failing at the other. Now see exactly why.

lesson.text:
Heart block after an infarct is this section in one patient, because the artery that is blocked tells you the level of the block.

Go back to the blood supply in the relay. The AV node is fed by the right coronary artery in about nine people in ten. Below it, the bundle of His and both bundle branches run down the septum, and the septum is fed by the septal branches of the left anterior descending artery. So an inferior infarct hurts the calcium node, and an anterior infarct hurts the sodium wiring. You could now predict the rest without the card.

The inferior infarct. Part of the block is not even damage. The inferior wall sets off a vagal reflex, and the ischaemic node is bathed in adenosine, both of which, you remember, open the same potassium channel and quieten the node. So you see first-degree block and Wenckebach. If it goes on to complete block there is a junctional pacemaker just beneath: a narrow escape at forty to sixty. It responds to atropine, and it usually recovers within days, especially once the artery is open.

The anterior infarct. To reach the bundles, the infarct has to destroy a large part of the septum, so this is a big infarct before the block even appears. The warnings are on the ECG: a new right bundle branch block, a new bifascicular block, which you will build in the next section, or Mobitz two. Then complete block, with only a wide ventricular escape slower than forty. Atropine does not reach it, and by speeding the atria it can make matters worse. This patient needs a pacing wire.

[[Inferior infarct: block in the node, narrow escape, atropine works, usually transient. Anterior infarct: block below the node, wide escape, atropine fails, pace.]]

Now the bank, and it has three traps. One, the statement that anterior infarction most commonly produces second and third-degree block. False, and only fifteen per cent saw it. Inferior infarction causes more block of every degree, complete block included. Anterior block is rarer and far more dangerous. Rarer, but worse. Two, the keyed true statement in that same item: AV block develops transiently in ten to twenty-five per cent of acute infarcts. If the inferior statement appears beside it and both are true, the transient one is the key. Three, the wrong key you have already met: block after an anterior infarct keyed as Mobitz one and atropine. Choose the His-Purkinje level and pacing.

For the patient who cannot tolerate the slow rate, the European steps are three: an intravenous chronotrope, then temporary pacing if that fails, and urgent angiography if he has not been reperfused, because opening the artery treats the cause. A permanent pacemaker waits. Most of these blocks recover, so it is considered only if high-degree block persists beyond about five days. The second ACS packet takes this up again at the bedside.

steps.bridge: When atropine cannot reach the block, the rate has to come from electricity. Three pacing decisions.

lesson.text:
A rate of thirty-six, a pressure of seventy-six over forty, a confused patient, and a strip showing sinus bradycardia. The answer is atropine, and you can now say why it is atropine, which is what protects you when the stem changes.

Atropine does not stimulate anything. It blocks the muscarinic receptor, so it takes the vagal hand off the heart. And the vagal hand, you remember, rests on the sinus node and the AV node and hardly touches the wiring below. So atropine is a bet that the slow rate is vagal and nodal. Most symptomatic bradycardia is, which is why the drug comes first.

The numbers on the card: one milligram intravenously, repeated every three to five minutes, to a total of three milligrams. At three the vagus is fully blocked and more adds only side effects. The European algorithm, and American keys written before twenty twenty, start with half a milligram, to the same ceiling of three. So if the options offer half a milligram and not one, half a milligram is the answer. A timid dose, under half a milligram, can paradoxically slow the heart. If atropine fails, the next step drives the beta receptor directly or bypasses conduction: dopamine, adrenaline or pacing. The infusion rates belong to the Rhythm packet, but keep one distinction, because only thirty-four per cent got it: dopamine is dosed per kilogram, adrenaline for bradycardia is two to ten micrograms a minute, with no per kilogram.

Now the two places where the bet is lost before you place it. The first is block below the node: Mobitz two, or complete block with a wide escape. There is no vagal hand there to remove. The second is the transplanted heart. The surgeon has cut its nerves, so there is no vagal tone to block. Atropine fails, glycopyrrolate fails, and ephedrine fails too, because it works largely by releasing noradrenaline from nerve endings that are no longer there. You need a drug that acts directly on the receptor, isoprenaline or adrenaline, or pacing. Marrow asked it: bradycardia years after a heart transplant, best drug? Isoprenaline.

[[Atropine only removes vagal tone. It is useless in block below the node and in the transplanted, denervated heart, where isoprenaline, adrenaline or pacing is needed.]]

Keep that denervated heart in mind. Later in this packet it turns out to be unusually sensitive to adenosine, for the same reason.

steps.bridge: Drugs, pads, a wire. But while you do any of it, ask why the heart slowed. Four causes, all reversible.

lesson.text:
Three decisions about pacing, and the first two are the level of the block once more.

Mobitz two with syncope and no reversible cause. It is disease of the sodium wiring, it goes to complete block without warning, and what is left underneath is the slow, unreliable ventricular escape. So once drugs, ischaemia and hyperkalaemia are excluded, the answer is a permanent pacemaker. The European pacing guideline gives Mobitz two a pacemaker even when the patient has no symptoms.

Complete block with shock. Pace, and the order matters. Transcutaneous pads now, because they take a minute. A transvenous wire next, because it is the better pacemaker and takes time to place. A chronotrope as the bridge. The grand test gave an unstable patient with Mobitz two and asked for the initial intervention, and only forty-three per cent chose transcutaneous pacing. NEET's favourite wrong option is the transvenous pacemaker. Atropine is the other wrong option, because it works on the node and not below it.

[[Unstable block below the node: transcutaneous pacing first, as the bridge to a transvenous wire. Symptomatic Mobitz two with no reversible cause ends in a permanent pacemaker.]]

The third decision is a child, and here the adult reasoning does not apply. An adult's bradycardia is usually a conduction problem. A child's is usually the last stage of hypoxia: a heart slowing because it is running out of oxygen. So the first move is to oxygenate and ventilate. If that has been done and the rate is still under sixty with poor perfusion, it is treated as an arrest about to happen: start compressions and give adrenaline, zero point zero one milligrams per kilogram. Only twenty-two per cent got this; the wrong options are atropine and dopamine, the adult reflexes.

And notice the exception inside the exception, which a later grand test asked. If the stem says the child's bradycardia is caused by raised vagal tone or by a primary AV block, the specifically indicated drug is atropine. The cause decides, in children as in adults.

steps.bridge: A blocked wire can also fail one branch at a time. Then no beat is dropped: the QRS just changes shape.

lesson.text:
One short card closes the story of the slow heart. While you give atropine and reach for the pads, you look for the cause at the same time, because the card's four categories are all reversible. And each one maps onto what you have built.

Ischaemia or infarction: the artery tells you the level, the right coronary for the node and the anterior descending for the wiring.

Drugs and toxins: calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and digoxin. All three act on the calcium node, so their effects add. Marrow asked it neatly: a patient on metoprolol for atrial fibrillation develops symptomatic bradycardia, and which other drug is the culprit working with it? Digoxin, which slows the node through the vagus. NEET's wrong reading is that the beta-blocker alone explains it.

Hypoxia: late and ominous, and in a child the usual cause, as you have just seen.

Electrolytes, above all hyperkalaemia. This one is different from the drugs. Potassium does not pick a level. It partly depolarises every cell, the sodium gates cannot reset, and conduction slows everywhere at once: sinus node, atria, AV node and ventricle. That is why a slow, wide, strange rhythm in a patient with kidney failure is hyperkalaemia until proven otherwise. It has its own section later in this packet.

[[Bradycardia has four reversible causes to look for at once: ischaemia, the nodal drugs, hypoxia and electrolytes, above all hyperkalaemia.]]

Each of the poisonings has its own antidote, and that is the business of the Cardiac drugs packet.

So far every failure has cost a whole beat. A P wave crossed or it did not. But below the bundle of His the wiring divides, and a block in one branch does something quieter. That is the next section.

spine: Two kinds of cell, two kinds of block: the calcium node tires gradually, the sodium wiring below it fails all at once.
Node: first degree and Mobitz I, narrow QRS, vagal, inferior MI, improves with atropine and exercise, benign.
Below the node: Mobitz II, constant PR, often wide QRS, anterior MI, atropine useless or harmful, needs pacing.
2:1 block cannot be classified by PR: QRS width, setting and response to atropine or exercise give the level.
Complete block is two independent clocks; the escape gives the level: narrow 40–60 junctional, wide 20–40 ventricular.
Treat by level: atropine for the node, pacing below it, and always look for ischaemia, drugs, hypoxia and potassium.

open.text:
The first packet gave you the wiring, the waves and the cameras, and you used them to find an injured wall. This packet asks the next three questions. What happens when the wiring itself fails? What happens when the circuit short-circuits? And what happens when a drug or an ion changes the cell?

Start with the sentence that takes the fear out of heart block. [[The level of the block decides everything. Block in the calcium node fatigues gradually and is usually benign. Block in the sodium wiring below it fails suddenly and is dangerous.]] Mobitz one and Mobitz two aren't two facts to memorise. They're the two kinds of cell you met at the very start, each failing in its own way.

Then the same idea one level lower, in the bundle branches and fascicles, and why a left bundle branch block hides an infarct. Then the short circuits: how a fast rhythm forms, and the shape each one draws on paper. Then the antiarrhythmic drugs, hung on the same action potential, so that each class becomes the phase it touches and the wave it changes. And last, what changes the waves from outside the wiring. Potassium, calcium and magnesium. The QT and torsades. And the poisons that write their names on the ECG: the tricyclics, digoxin, the beta-blockers and the calcium-channel blockers.

Many of these were exam losses for you. Wolff–Parkinson–White, the AV block statements, the vagal manoeuvres, the Schwartz score, the safe drug in long QT, the tricyclic in a child, and digoxin Fab during an arrest. Each one has its place in this packet, and by the end each should feel obvious.

Listen for the same three ions. Sodium, calcium, potassium. They're still doing all the work.

Begin with the slow heart, and the gate that decides how slow.

questions.text: One level lower: bundle branches, fascicles and the paced heart

open.text:
A bundle branch block is not a new topic. It is Mobitz two's disease, the broken sodium wire, met one level lower and one wire at a time. That is the idea to hold through this section.

Below the bundle of His the wiring divides into a right bundle and a left bundle. When the single trunk above them fails, a whole beat is lost. When only one branch fails, nothing is lost. The impulse goes down the healthy branch, and the ventricle on the blocked side is reached late, the slow way, from muscle cell to muscle cell. So the PR is unchanged. What changes is the QRS: it is wide, because one ventricle finishes late, and it has a new shape, because the late wave travels in a new direction.

You already own the tool for the shape. A wave coming towards a camera is upright, a wave going away is downward. With one camera at V1 on the right and one at V6 on the left, you can draw both blocks yourself.

The trap to listen for: a left bundle branch block lifts the ST segment in V1 to V3 every day of the patient's life, so it can hide an infarct. Start with the two branches.

steps.bridge: The left bundle is two wires, not one. Block a single fascicle and the QRS stays narrow, but the axis swings.

lesson.text:
Start from the normal sequence, because a bundle branch block is that sequence with one part delayed.

You will remember that the septum fires first, from left to right, because the first fibres to leave the wiring come off the left bundle. Then both ventricles are activated together, and since the left ventricle is so much thicker, the main wave points to the left. From V1, on the right, that is a small wave coming towards the camera and then a large one going away: small r, deep S. From V6, on the left, it is the mirror: a small septal q, then a tall R.

Now block the right bundle. The septum and the left ventricle are activated normally, so the first part of the QRS is unchanged. But the right ventricle has received nothing. The wave has to creep across through muscle, and it arrives late, after the left ventricle has finished, with nothing left to oppose it. So the QRS ends with an extra wave travelling to the right. Towards V1: a second upright wave, called R prime. Away from V6 and lead one: a wide, slurred S wave. So V1 shows r, S, R prime, the shape of a letter M. The axis stays normal, because the left ventricle was activated normally.

Now block the left bundle, and something more fundamental changes: the beginning. The septum can no longer be fired from the left, so it is fired from the right bundle, right to left. The small septal q in lead one and V6 disappears. Then the wave works slowly through the thick left ventricle, all of it travelling leftward. So V6 and lead one show a broad, notched, entirely upright R wave, and V1 to V3 show a deep, wide, downward complex. Often the axis is to the left.

{{**Bundle branch block: QRS ≥ 0.12 s**
 | V1 | V6, lead I
RBBB | rSR′ ("M") | wide slurred S
LBBB | deep QS or rS | broad notched R, no septal q
Incomplete block | same shape, QRS 0.10–0.12 s}}

The classic aid is the pair of words William and Marrow. William, with its two letters L, is the left bundle: a W in V1 and an M in V6. Marrow, with its two letters R, is the right: an M in V1 and a W in V6. Complete block is a QRS of zero point one two seconds or more. The same shape between zero point one zero and zero point one two is called incomplete.

Next, the ST segment and T wave. When depolarisation takes an abnormal route, repolarisation does too, and the ST segment and T wave point away from the last part of the QRS. This secondary change is expected. In right bundle branch block the QRS ends upright in V1, so T inversion in V1 to V3 is normal for it. In left bundle branch block the QRS is downward in V1 to V3, so the ST segment there is lifted and the T is upright, and in V6 the ST is depressed and the T inverted. NEET's favourite wrong reading is to call that ST elevation in V1 to V3 an anterior infarct. A real infarct can hide behind it, and the last two cards of this section find it.

[[The late wave points to the blocked side. Right bundle: an extra R prime in V1 and a slurred S in V6. Left bundle: a broad notched R in V6, a deep QS in V1, and no septal q.]]

What each one means. A right bundle branch block can be found in a healthy heart, or with a strained right ventricle, as in pulmonary embolism or an atrial septal defect. And a new one in an anterior infarct means a proximal occlusion of the anterior descending artery, whose septal branches feed that bundle. A left bundle branch block almost always means a diseased left ventricle: hypertension, coronary disease, cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis.

Two look-alikes. A pacing wire sits at the apex of the right ventricle, so a paced beat starts on the right and spreads leftward: a pacing spike, then a wide complex of left bundle shape. And at fast rates a beat can reach a bundle that is still refractory, usually the right one, which recovers more slowly. That is a bundle branch block only at speed, called aberrant conduction. You will need it for the wide tachycardias later.

[[In bundle branch block the ST segment and T wave point away from the last part of the QRS. ST elevation in V1 to V3 is expected in left bundle branch block.]]
lesson.cap: RBBB: rsR′ in V1, wide S in I and V6. LBBB: broad notched R in I and V6, QS in V1, ST-T opposite to the QRS.

steps.bridge: Left bundle branch block hides an infarct behind its own ST elevation. Sgarbossa asked what the block cannot do.

lesson.text:
The ventricles are really fed by three wires. The right bundle is one. The left bundle is a short trunk that fans into two: an anterior fascicle to the front and top of the left ventricle, and a posterior fascicle to the back and bottom. The anterior fascicle is long and thin, with a single blood supply from the anterior descending artery, so it is blocked often. The posterior is short and broad, with a double supply, so it is blocked rarely.

What happens when one fascicle fails? The left ventricle is still reached through the other one, and the Purkinje network connects the two regions, so the delay is small and the QRS hardly widens. What changes is the order. The region served by the blocked fascicle is activated last, and the last, unopposed wave decides the axis. You met this as the third rule of axis: in a block, the axis swings towards the region activated late.

Left anterior fascicular block. Activation starts through the posterior fascicle, downward, and then sweeps up and to the left, towards the late anterior and superior wall. So the axis is left, at minus forty-five degrees or beyond. In the leads: lead one and aVL see a small q and then a tall R, and lead two, three and aVF see a small r and then a deep S. This is the commonest single cause of left axis deviation.

Left posterior fascicular block is the mirror. Activation starts upward through the anterior fascicle and then sweeps down and to the right. So the axis is right, beyond plus ninety degrees, with a small r and deep S in lead one and aVL, and a small q and tall R in the inferior leads. Because it is rare, it is a diagnosis you make only after excluding the common causes of right axis: right ventricular hypertrophy, a lateral infarct and pulmonary embolism.

{{**Fascicular blocks: QRS < 0.12 s**
 | Axis | I, aVL | II, III, aVF
LAFB | left, −45° or beyond | qR | rS
LPFB | right, +90° or beyond | rS | qR
Bifascicular = RBBB + one fascicle (LAFB commonest)}}

One mimic. An old inferior infarct also gives a left axis with downward complexes in the inferior leads. The difference is the first wave. In left anterior fascicular block the inferior leads begin with a small r. In an inferior infarct they begin with a Q, because the dead wall is a window.

Now count wires. Bifascicular block means two of the three are out. The commonest form is right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block: a right bundle pattern with a left axis. Both wires are fed by the anterior descending artery, which is why the pair appears in a large anterior infarct. Every beat now depends on one remaining wire.

Trifascicular block, strictly, means disease in all three. That is either complete heart block, or the finding that proves it: right bundle branch block on one strip and left bundle branch block on another. This is alternating bundle branch block. If each bundle fails some of the time, a moment will come when both fail together. The European pacing guideline of twenty twenty-one gives it a class one recommendation for a permanent pacemaker, with or without symptoms.

[[Alternating bundle branch block means all three wires are failing: a permanent pacemaker, even without symptoms. Right bundle branch block with a left axis is bifascicular block.]]

You will also hear trifascicular block used loosely for bifascicular block with a long PR. Be careful. The long PR may be only a tired node above the damaged wires, which is much milder. A recording from inside the heart can tell. It measures the H to V interval, the time from the bundle of His to the ventricle, normally about thirty-five to fifty-five milliseconds. So for the patient with bifascicular block and unexplained syncope, the answer is an electrophysiology study, and an H to V interval of seventy milliseconds or more means a pacemaker.

[[Left anterior fascicular block: left axis with a small r and deep S in the inferior leads. An inferior infarct also gives left axis, but its inferior leads begin with a Q.]]
lesson.cap: LAFB: axis −45° or beyond, qR in aVL, rS in II, III, aVF. LPFB: right axis, rS in I and aVL, qR inferiorly — exclude RVH, PE, lateral MI first.

steps.bridge: Sgarbossa is specific but misses most infarcts. Smith made it sensitive, and the pathway puts the patient first.

lesson.text:
Now the problem you were warned about. In left bundle branch block the ST segment is displaced in every lead, all the time, away from the main direction of the QRS. Where the QRS is downward, as in V1 to V3, the ST is up. Where the QRS is upright, as in V6, the ST is down. This is called appropriate discordance, and it makes the ordinary one millimetre rule for infarction useless.

Elena Sgarbossa's idea, from the nineteen nineties, was simple: stop looking for ST elevation, and look for what a bundle branch block cannot do. There are three findings.

The first is concordant ST elevation: one millimetre or more of ST elevation in a lead where the QRS is upright. The block should have pushed that ST segment down. Only an injury current can lift it. Five points.

The second is concordant ST depression of one millimetre or more in V1, V2 or V3. Those leads have a downward QRS, so their ST should be up. ST depression there is the wrong direction. Three points. And you may recognise it as the picture of a posterior infarct seen through the block.

The third is discordant ST elevation of five millimetres or more in a lead with a downward QRS. That is the right direction, only too much of it. Since it is merely an exaggeration of normal, it scores least. Two points.

{{**Sgarbossa (LBBB or ventricular paced rhythm)**
Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm, QRS positive | **5**
Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1–V3 | **3**
Discordant ST elevation ≥ 5 mm, QRS negative | **2**
**≥ 3** = infarction, specificity > 90%}}

A score of three or more diagnoses infarction with a specificity above ninety per cent. Work out what that means: either concordant finding is enough alone, and the five millimetre finding alone is not.

[[Sgarbossa: concordant ST elevation scores five, concordant ST depression in V1 to V3 scores three, discordant elevation of five millimetres scores two. Three or more rules infarction in.]]

The trap runs the other way. The score is specific, not sensitive. It finds only about a fifth to a third of infarcts, so a score of zero excludes nothing. NEET's wrong statement is that a normal Sgarbossa score rules out infarction.

Two last points. A ventricular paced rhythm, you now know, is drawn like a left bundle branch block, so the same criteria apply to it, though with less certainty. And a new left bundle branch block, taken alone, is no longer treated as an infarct. Most such patients have no blocked artery. It warrants investigation, and what you do with the patient in front of you is the next card.
lesson.cap: Sgarbossa in LBBB or RV pacing: concordant ST↑ ≥ 1 mm (5), concordant ST↓ ≥ 1 mm in V1–V3 (3), discordant ST↑ ≥ 5 mm (2); ≥ 3 points = MI.

steps.bridge: Slow rhythms and wide beats are done. Now the fast ones: nearly every one is an impulse caught in a loop.

lesson.text:
A patient arrives with chest pain and a left bundle branch block. The pathway on this card asks three questions in order, and a yes to any one of them means reperfusion.

The first question is not about the ECG. Is the patient haemodynamically unstable, or in acute heart failure? If so, stop there and reperfuse. The grand test asked this branch: chest pain, new left bundle branch block, hypotension and shock. Treat as a STEMI equivalent, and nine in ten were right. The wrong options are the patient ones, repeating the ECG or trending the troponin.

The second question is Sgarbossa: a score of three or more.

The third is the refinement added by Stephen Smith. Sgarbossa's weakest criterion used a fixed five millimetres, and that ignores the size of the complex. A huge S wave drags up a large ST segment quite innocently, and a small S wave does not. So Smith measured the ST elevation as a proportion of the S wave in front of it. If the ST elevation is a quarter or more of the depth of the S wave, the discordance is excessive. The card writes it as a ratio of ST to S of minus zero point two five or beyond, and the minus sign is there only because the two point in opposite directions. Scaling the rule this way makes it far more sensitive, about eighty to ninety per cent in the studies, without losing specificity.

[[Left bundle branch block with chest pain: instability, a Sgarbossa score of three or more, or ST elevation of a quarter or more of the S wave each mean reperfusion.]]

If all three answers are no, most of these patients do not have an occlusion, so you let time work: serial ECGs, serial troponins and a bedside echo looking for a wall that does not move. Abnormal, and the patient goes for angiography. Normal, and a non-invasive evaluation follows.

The paced patient is handled the same way, and the same ratio has been tested in paced rhythms. The European guideline of twenty twenty-three puts it in one sentence: a bundle branch block or a paced rhythm, with a strong clinical suspicion of ongoing ischaemia, is managed like a STEMI. The first ACS packet walks this pathway again with the patient in front of you.

That finishes the slow heart and the wide beat. Everything so far was an impulse failing to get through. The opposite fault is an impulse that will not stop.

spine: Below the His bundle a block in one branch drops no beat: the QRS widens and its last part points to the blocked side.
RBBB: rSR′ in V1, slurred S in V6 and lead I. LBBB: broad notched R in V6, QS in V1, no septal q. RV pacing looks like LBBB.
Secondary ST–T points away from the QRS, so ST elevation in V1–V3 is expected in LBBB.
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow but swings the axis: LAFB left, LPFB right. RBBB + left axis = bifascicular block.
Alternating bundle branch block = pacemaker (class I). Bifascicular block with syncope: EP study, HV ≥ 70 ms = pacemaker.
Infarct behind LBBB or pacing: concordance (Sgarbossa ≥ 3) or ST/S ≤ −0.25; unstable with ischaemic pain = treat as STEMI.

questions.text: Short circuits: how fast rhythms form, and the shape each one draws

open.text:
A fast rhythm is usually not a pacemaker firing faster. It is a single impulse that has found a loop and keeps going round it. That one idea separates two things you may have filed together, the sinus tachycardia of a septic patient and the sudden tachycardia at one hundred and eighty, and it unites a long list you may have learned as separate names: AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter and most ventricular tachycardia are all the same event, an impulse circling, in four different places.

So the question of this section is the question of the last two, asked of a loop. Where is it? In the blocks, the level decided everything. Here the place of the loop decides the shape on the ECG, and it decides what will stop it. If the loop passes through the AV node, the calcium gate, then anything that closes the gate for a few seconds ends the rhythm. If the loop lies elsewhere, closing the gate only lets you see it better.

The trap to listen for is the one heart where closing the gate is dangerous: a heart with a second road around it. First, the three ways a rhythm can go wrong at all.

steps.bridge: The commonest loop is the smallest: a circuit inside the AV node itself, with its P wave hidden in the QRS.

lesson.text:
Every abnormal rhythm, fast or early, starts in one of three ways, and you already have the physiology for each.

The first is automaticity. A pacemaker fires faster, or cells that should not fire at all begin to. Go back to the pacemaker potential: the rate depends on the slope of phase four, and catecholamines, fever, hypoxia, ischaemia and a low potassium all steepen it. Sinus tachycardia is the plain example. A focal atrial tachycardia is the same thing in the wrong place, and so is the wide, harmless rhythm at fifty to a hundred or so a minute that appears when a blocked artery reopens, the accelerated idioventricular rhythm. Automatic rhythms warm up and cool down gradually. You treat the cause, and a shock does nothing lasting, because the cells simply fire again.

The second is triggered activity: a beat provoked by the beat before it, in two kinds. An early afterdepolarisation happens before repolarisation is finished, in phase two or three. It needs a long action potential, so that calcium channels have time to recover and reopen, and that means a long QT, made worse by a slow rate, a low potassium or a low magnesium. This is the trigger of torsades de pointes. A delayed afterdepolarisation happens after repolarisation is complete, when the cell is overloaded with calcium and leaks it. That is digoxin toxicity and catecholamine excess, and its signature is bidirectional ventricular tachycardia.

The third, and by far the commonest cause of a sustained tachycardia, is re-entry. Picture a ring road around a town, entered at the top. An impulse arriving there splits, runs down both sides, and the two halves meet at the bottom and cancel. Nothing happens. For a loop to form you need two things. One side must be blocked in the forward direction, because it is still refractory from the last beat. And conduction down the other side must be slow enough that, by the time the impulse reaches the bottom, the blocked side has recovered. Then the impulse turns up the recovered side, arrives back at the top, and goes round again, and each lap fires the rest of the heart.

[[Re-entry needs two pathways, block in one direction down one of them, and conduction slow enough in the other for the first to recover. It starts and stops abruptly.]]

That explains its behaviour. It starts suddenly, with one early beat that catches one side refractory. It runs at a fixed rate, the time of one lap. And it stops suddenly when any part of the ring is made refractory. Where is the ring? In AVNRT it is inside the AV node. In AVRT it is the node together with an accessory pathway. In flutter it is a large circuit around the tricuspid valve in the right atrium. In ventricular tachycardia after an infarct it runs through the edge of the scar.

So here is the rule for breaking a tachycardia. If the node is part of the ring, a vagal manoeuvre or adenosine closes the node for a moment and the rhythm ends. If the node is only a bystander, as in flutter or atrial tachycardia, closing it does not stop the atria. It only slows the ventricles for a few seconds and unmasks the atrial rhythm.

Now the grid, which a grand test asked and most of the cohort got right. Ask two questions of any tachycardia. Is the QRS narrow or wide? Narrow means the ventricles are activated down the normal wiring, so the rhythm comes from above them. And is it regular or irregular?

{{**The 2 × 2 grid**
 | Regular | Irregular
Narrow | sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT, atrial tachycardia, flutter with fixed block | AF, flutter with variable block, MAT
Wide | VT, SVT with bundle branch block, antidromic AVRT | pre-excited AF, AF with bundle branch block, polymorphic VT}}

Two lines from the grid are worth more than the rest. A loop through the node is always regular, so AVNRT and AVRT never appear in the irregular column. And wide with irregular holds the two rhythms where the usual drugs can kill: pre-excited atrial fibrillation and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

[[A node-dependent loop, AVNRT or AVRT, is always regular and ends with adenosine. An irregular narrow tachycardia is atrial: fibrillation, flutter with variable block, or multifocal atrial tachycardia.]]
lesson.cap: Re-entry needs two paths, one-way block and slow conduction. Sort every tachycardia by narrow or wide, regular or irregular.

steps.bridge: AVRT needed a second road between atrium and ventricle. In sinus rhythm that road signs the ECG: the delta wave.

lesson.text:
Regular, narrow, one hundred and eighty a minute, no visible P waves, patient stable. From the grid this is a loop through the node, and the commonest one is AVNRT. Here is how it forms, because the mechanism draws the ECG.

In many people the AV node has two ways through it. A fast pathway, which conducts quickly but recovers slowly. And a slow pathway, which conducts slowly but recovers quickly. That is exactly the pair re-entry needs. In sinus rhythm the fast pathway carries every beat. Then an early atrial beat arrives while the fast pathway is still refractory. It can only go down the slow one. By the time it reaches the bottom, the fast pathway has recovered, so the impulse runs back up it to the atria while also continuing down to the ventricles. Down the slow, up the fast, round and round.

Because the turning point is inside the node, the impulse reaches the atria and the ventricles at almost the same moment. So the P wave is fired at the same time as the QRS and hides inside it, or just peeps out at its tail: a small false S wave in the inferior leads and a small false r prime in V1. The gap from the R wave to that P is tiny, under about seventy milliseconds. And if you can see the P at all, it is inverted in lead two, three and aVF, because the atria are being activated from below, away from those cameras.

That last point caught most people. A grand test showed a regular tachycardia at one hundred and eighty with inverted P waves in the inferior leads and asked the mechanism. Only forty-two per cent chose re-entry within the AV node. NEET's wrong option was re-entry through an accessory pathway.

That is AVRT, and the one discriminator is distance. In AVRT the ring is much bigger: down the node, through the ventricle, up an accessory pathway at the side of the heart, and back through the atrium. The impulse has to cross ventricular muscle before it can climb back, so the P wave comes later, clearly separate, sitting in the ST segment. The gap from R to P is more than seventy milliseconds. Both rhythms are regular, and both contain the node, so both end with adenosine.

[[AVNRT hides its P wave in or at the tail of the QRS: a false S in the inferior leads, a false r prime in V1. AVRT shows a separate P in the ST segment. Both stop with adenosine.]]

The third mimic, focal atrial tachycardia, has a P wave in front of each QRS and carries on when the node is blocked.

The treatment ladder is the Rhythm packet's work, so only its logic here. Close the gate: a vagal manoeuvre first, then adenosine. One item gave a stable patient at one hundred and eighty and asked the first step, and only half chose the vagal manoeuvre over adenosine. And one exception has the lowest score in the whole series. The patient is asthmatic. Adenosine can provoke bronchospasm, so you close the same gate by another route. The node is a calcium tissue, so verapamil or diltiazem blocks it just as surely and leaves the airway alone. On the mini test seven per cent chose it.

[[Supraventricular tachycardia in an asthmatic: verapamil or diltiazem in place of adenosine, provided the ventricle is normal and there is no pre-excitation.]]
lesson.cap: AVNRT: P hidden at the end of the QRS (pseudo-r′ in V1), RP < 70 ms. Orthodromic AVRT: P in the ST segment, RP > 70 ms.

steps.bridge: Twice now the answer was to close the node, by the vagus or by adenosine. They are two keys to one lock.

lesson.text:
The AV node, you remember, is a deliberate delay and a deliberate brake. The faster it is driven, the more slowly it conducts. In Wolff-Parkinson-White there is a second connection between atrium and ventricle, a strand of ordinary sodium muscle that bypasses the node. It has no delay and no brake.

In sinus rhythm you can see it. The impulse goes down both routes at once. The accessory pathway does not wait, so a patch of ventricle is activated early: the PR is short, under zero point one two seconds. That early wave spreads slowly, from muscle cell to muscle cell, so the first part of the QRS is slurred. That is the delta wave. Then the impulse that went through the node arrives down the fast wiring and finishes the job. So the QRS is a fusion of the two, a little wide, with ST and T changes pointing the other way, as in a bundle branch block. A downward delta wave can pass for the Q wave of an old infarct, and a left-sided pathway gives one of the tall R waves in V1. A grand test asked what lies behind a short PR and a delta wave, and only thirty-nine per cent chose an accessory AV pathway. The wrong option was a dual AV nodal pathway, which is AVNRT and leaves the resting ECG normal.

Two roads between atrium and ventricle make a ring, so three tachycardias are possible. Sort them by which road carries the impulse down.

Down the node and back up the pathway is orthodromic AVRT, by far the commonest. The ventricles are activated through the normal wiring, so it is narrow and regular, and the delta wave vanishes during the attack. The node is in the ring, so this is treated like any other loop through the node: a vagal manoeuvre, then adenosine, then a drug that blocks the node. That was the keyed sequence in a grand test that only a third got right, because people had learned never to block the node in this syndrome. The ban belongs to a different rhythm.

Down the pathway and back up the node is antidromic AVRT, which is rare, wide and regular, and looks like ventricular tachycardia.

The third is the dangerous one: atrial fibrillation in a patient with a pathway. The atria fire at four hundred or more. The node would let through perhaps one hundred and fifty. The pathway, with no brake, can pass up to three hundred. So the rhythm is irregular, very fast and wide, and the QRS changes width from beat to beat, each one a different mix of pathway and node. Now block the node. The beats that came down the node used to enter the pathway from below and keep it partly refractory. Remove them, and the pathway carries everything, and the ventricle fibrillates.

[[In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, block the pathway, never the node: cardioversion if unstable, procainamide or ibutilide if stable. No adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blocker, digoxin or intravenous amiodarone.]]

Intravenous amiodarone is on that list because its early effect is mostly on the node, and both the European and the American guidelines class it as harmful here. Twice a grand test has asked for the contraindicated drug with verapamil as the key, while adenosine, esmolol and amiodarone sat among the options. Mark verapamil, the classic answer.

One discriminator for the strip. Ventricular tachycardia is regular with identical complexes. Pre-excited fibrillation is irregular with complexes of changing width, in a young patient.

Last, the card's own drug, flecainide. It is a sodium channel blocker, so it slows the sodium muscle of the pathway and prevents attacks. It is forbidden in a diseased or infarcted ventricle, and its commonest side effect outside the heart is blurred vision. The cure is catheter ablation of the pathway.

[[Orthodromic AVRT in Wolff-Parkinson-White is narrow and regular with the node in the loop: vagal manoeuvre, adenosine, then a nodal blocker. The ban on nodal blockers is for the irregular wide rhythm.]]
lesson.cap: WPW: short PR + delta wave. Orthodromic AVRT is narrow (node in the loop: vagal, adenosine). Pre-excited AF is fast, irregular, wide: no nodal blockers.

steps.bridge: Adenosine stops a loop through the node. When the loop is in the atrium it only reveals it: flutter is the classic.

lesson.text:
A vagal manoeuvre and adenosine look like two unrelated treatments, one a trick of posture and one a drug. They are two keys to the same lock.

Go back to the autonomic hands. The vagus releases acetylcholine onto the muscarinic receptor of the nodal cell, and that opens a potassium channel. Potassium leaves, the cell is pulled away from threshold, and the node stops conducting. Adenosine binds its own receptor, the A one receptor, on the same cell, and opens that same potassium channel. So both do one thing: for a few seconds they hold the calcium gate shut. Any loop that runs through the gate is broken. And neither touches the sodium wiring or the ventricular muscle, which is why neither is a treatment for ventricular tachycardia.

Now the fine print, which was asked as a set of statements and missed.

The Valsalva manoeuvre works on release. While the patient strains, pressure in the chest rises, venous return falls and the blood pressure sags. On letting go, blood surges back, the pressure overshoots, the baroreceptors fire and the vagus slows the node. The modified version makes the surge bigger: strain at forty millimetres of mercury for fifteen seconds, sitting half upright, then lie flat at once with the legs lifted. In the REVERT trial that restored sinus rhythm in forty-three per cent against seventeen per cent for the standard manoeuvre. The false statement on offer is to take a deep breath before straining. It is a sustained strain.

Carotid sinus massage presses on the baroreceptor directly. Supine, on a monitor, one side only, for five to ten seconds. Never both sides, and never with a carotid bruit or a previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack, because fingers can dislodge plaque.

[[The vagus and adenosine open the same potassium channel in the AV node. Carotid massage is one-sided, five to ten seconds, and never with a bruit or a previous stroke.]]

Adenosine's rules come from its half-life, under ten seconds, because red cells and vessel walls take it up at once. So it is pushed fast into a large vein and chased with a flush. And the dose falls whenever more of it reaches the receptor, or the receptor is more sensitive: through a central line, with dipyridamole, which blocks its uptake, with carbamazepine, and in the transplanted heart, which, having lost its nerves, over-responds. The exam answer for the reduced first dose is three milligrams, and the current American guideline says one milligram may be enough through a central line or after a transplant. In the other direction, theophylline and caffeine block its receptor, so more may be needed.

One last use. In a wide tachycardia that is regular and monomorphic, adenosine is allowed as a test: if it was a loop through the node with a bundle branch block, it stops, and if it was ventricular, nothing happens. But never in a wide tachycardia that is irregular or polymorphic. You know why: that may be pre-excited fibrillation, and you would be closing the node.

[[Adenosine: reduce the first dose through a central line, after a heart transplant, or with dipyridamole or carbamazepine. Never give it for an irregular or polymorphic wide tachycardia.]]

steps.bridge: All of these were narrow because they came from above. A rhythm that starts in the ventricle is wide: how to prove it.

lesson.text:
Three atrial rhythms now, and in all three the node is only a bystander, deciding how much of the atrial activity gets through.

Flutter first. It is re-entry around one large, fixed ring: the impulse circles the right atrium round the tricuspid valve, through a narrow strip of muscle between that valve and the inferior vena cava. One lap takes a fifth of a second, so the atrial rate is about three hundred a minute, one flutter wave for every large square. The atrium is never at rest, so there is no flat baseline: the waves run together as a sawtooth, downward in lead two, three and aVF and upright in V1.

The node cannot conduct three hundred. It usually passes every second wave, so the ventricles beat at one hundred and fifty, regular and narrow. That number is the clue.

[[A regular narrow tachycardia at almost exactly one hundred and fifty a minute is atrial flutter with two to one conduction until proven otherwise.]]

One flutter wave hides in the QRS or the T wave, which is why it is missed. Close the node for a few seconds and the ventricles pause, the sawtooth stands alone, and then the tachycardia resumes. Adenosine reveals flutter. It never cures it. And if the node's share varies from beat to beat, flutter becomes irregular.

One drug point. Flecainide slows conduction around the ring, so the flutter rate may fall to about two hundred. That is slow enough for the node to conduct every wave, one to one, so the ventricular rate rises, with a wide QRS. So flecainide is given together with a drug that blocks the node.

Atrial fibrillation is not one ring but chaos: many small wavelets, at three hundred and fifty to six hundred a minute. There is no organised atrial contraction, so there are no P waves, only a fine or coarse wobble of the baseline. The node is bombarded at random and conducts at random, so the QRS complexes are narrow and irregularly irregular.

Two consequences follow. The first is the loss of the atrial kick. A normal ventricle hardly notices. A stiff ventricle depends on it for its final filling. So when a patient with severe aortic stenosis goes into fast atrial fibrillation and is in pulmonary oedema within hours, the mechanism is loss of atrial systole. A grand test asked this, and the tempting wrong option was acute coronary thrombosis. The second is at the bedside: no atrial contraction means no a wave in the neck veins or on the central venous trace. Compare complete heart block, with its cannon a waves.

Three patterns inside atrial fibrillation are worth a mark each. A wide beat that ends a short cycle following a long one is the Ashman phenomenon: the long cycle lengthens the refractory period of the right bundle, and the next early beat finds it shut. It is aberrant conduction, not a ventricular ectopic. Second, very fast fibrillation with wide complexes of varying shape is pre-excitation. Third, fibrillation in which the ventricles have become slow and perfectly regular. The node cannot conduct chaos regularly, so it is not conducting at all: this is complete heart block with a junctional escape, and on digoxin it means toxicity.

Last, multifocal atrial tachycardia. This one is automaticity, not re-entry: several irritable atrial foci firing in turn. So there are P waves, of at least three different shapes, with changing PR intervals, at a rate over one hundred, and the rhythm is irregular. It is the rhythm of the sick lung: chronic obstructive disease, hypoxia, theophylline, a low potassium or magnesium. You treat the lung and the electrolytes. A shock does not help.

{{**Atrial rhythms**
Flutter | sawtooth F waves ~300, no baseline; 2:1 gives 150 regular
AF | no P waves, irregularly irregular, atria 350–600
MAT | ≥ 3 P-wave shapes, rate > 100, irregular; lung disease}}

[[Irregularly irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation. Irregular with three or more shapes of P wave is multifocal atrial tachycardia. Slow and regular fibrillation on digoxin is complete block.]]
lesson.cap: Flutter: sawtooth at 300, usually 2:1 = 150. AF: no P, irregularly irregular. MAT: ≥ 3 P-wave shapes, irregular, rate > 100.

steps.bridge: One organised loop in the ventricle still gives a pulse sometimes. Break it into wavelets and there is nothing.

lesson.text:
Every rhythm so far began above the ventricles and came down the fast wiring, so the QRS was narrow unless a bundle was blocked. Now start the impulse in the ventricle itself.

It has no fast route. It spreads from muscle cell to muscle cell, slowly, so the QRS is wide. If it comes from one loop, usually around the edge of an old infarct scar, it takes the same path on every lap, so every complex in a lead looks the same and the rhythm is regular. That is the card: monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is a regular, broad complex tachycardia with identical complexes.

The difficulty is the mimic. A supraventricular tachycardia with a bundle branch block, fixed or brought on by the rate, is also wide and regular. How do you prove the ventricle is the source?

The proof is independence. In ventricular tachycardia the sinus node usually carries on firing the atria at its own slower rate. It is the two clocks again, with the lower clock the faster one this time. If you can see P waves marching through at their own rate, unrelated to the QRS, that is AV dissociation, and it settles the diagnosis. Two special beats show the same thing. Now and then a sinus impulse finds the node and the ventricle ready, and captures the ventricle by itself: one normal narrow beat in the middle of the run, a capture beat. Or it meets the ventricular wave halfway and the two share the ventricle: a hybrid, a fusion beat. So the card's exception to uniformity is also the strongest evidence.

[[A regular broad tachycardia with identical complexes is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. AV dissociation, capture beats and fusion beats prove it.]]

The supporting clues all say the same thing, that this wave is not using the wiring. The QRS is very wide, beyond zero point one four seconds with a right bundle shape or zero point one six with a left bundle shape, wider than a bundle branch block alone would make it. The axis is extreme, pointing up and to the right, the corner no normal wiring ever aims at. And the chest leads are concordant: V1 to V6 all upright or all downward. You may see these collected under the names of the Brugada algorithm, which adds a slow descent from the R wave to the bottom of the S wave of more than a hundred milliseconds, and the Vereckei algorithm, which uses aVR alone. You need the names, not the steps.

The safest clue is the patient. With a previous infarct or structural heart disease, a wide regular tachycardia is ventricular until proven otherwise. The grand test stem was ischaemic heart disease, chest pain, a wide QRS, no P waves and a rate of one hundred and fifty. The wrong options were flutter and atrial fibrillation.

And the rule for when you cannot decide: treat it as ventricular tachycardia. The treatments for ventricular tachycardia are safe in a supraventricular rhythm. The reverse is not true. Verapamil given to ventricular tachycardia in the belief that it is supraventricular can cause collapse.

[[A wide regular tachycardia in a patient with a previous infarct is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise. If in doubt, treat as ventricular tachycardia, and never give verapamil.]]
lesson.cap: VT proof: AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats. Wide regular tachycardia after MI = VT until proven otherwise.

steps.bridge: Loops, triggers and automatic foci: each has a weak point on the action potential. The drugs are named after it.

lesson.text:
Ventricular tachycardia is one loop. Ventricular fibrillation is what follows when that loop breaks up into many small wandering wavelets, each re-entering wherever it finds recovered muscle. You may remember the vulnerable period near the peak of the T wave, when some muscle has recovered and some has not: an early beat landing there is how the break-up begins.

The card describes what the cameras see. Chaotic, irregular deflections of varying height. No P waves, no QRS complexes, no T waves that you can identify, because nothing organised is happening. A rate, if you can call it that, of one hundred and fifty to five hundred a minute. It is not a heart rate. It is only how fast the line wobbles, and no wobble produces a contraction. So there is no output and no pulse, which the grand test asked plainly: the rhythm that cannot support perfusion.

The last line of the card is a clock. The waves start coarse and become fine as the muscle runs out of energy. Fine fibrillation means a longer time down and a poorer outlook. NEET's wrong statement is that fine fibrillation is too late to shock. It is still shocked. Its mimic is asystole, so before calling a flat line, check the leads and turn up the gain.

[[Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic deflections with no identifiable P, QRS or T, and no output. Coarse becomes fine with time, and fine fibrillation is still shocked.]]

What to do in the arrest belongs to the Arrest packet. For now you have the whole map of rhythms: a tired gate, a broken wire, a late branch, and an impulse caught in a loop. What remains is the drugs, and they hang on the same action potential you already know.

spine: Rhythms go wrong in three ways: automaticity (steeper phase 4), triggered beats (afterdepolarisations) and re-entry (a loop).
Where the loop lies decides the ECG: node (AVNRT, P hidden), node plus pathway (AVRT, P in ST), right atrium (flutter), scar (VT).
Vagus and adenosine close the node: a loop through it stops; flutter and atrial tachycardia are only unmasked.
WPW: short PR, delta wave. Orthodromic AVRT is treated through the node; pre-excited AF never is: procainamide or shock.
Regular narrow 150 = flutter 2:1. No P and irregularly irregular = AF. Three P shapes = MAT. Slow regular AF on digoxin = block.
Wide and regular with AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats = VT. If in doubt treat as VT; never verapamil.

questions.text: Antiarrhythmics hung on the same action potential

open.text:
The four classes of antiarrhythmic drug are not a list to memorise. They are the currents of the action potential, which you already know, with one class of drug sitting on each. Sodium, the sympathetic drive, potassium, calcium. That is all the Vaughan Williams classification is.

And because you tied each current to a part of the ECG, you can predict what every class does to the strip. You said it earlier as a single line: the QRS is sodium, the T wave is potassium, and the node is calcium. So a sodium blocker widens the QRS. A potassium blocker lengthens the QT. And the two classes that act on the calcium node, the beta-blockers and the calcium channel blockers, slow the rate and lengthen the PR. The dangers are the same sentence read again: widen the QRS too far and you build a new loop, lengthen the QT too far and you set off torsades.

So this section has two jobs. First, to hang each drug on its current. Second, to answer what the exam really asks, which is which drug this particular heart must never be given. Listen for that word, never.

steps.bridge: You know what each class does to the cell. The exam asks something harder: which heart must never get which drug.

lesson.text:
Walk along the action potential. Phase zero is sodium rushing in. Phase three is potassium leaving. In the node the upstroke is calcium, and phase four is the slope the sympathetic nerves steepen. Four handles, four classes. The classic aid for the order is the sentence some block potassium channels: sodium blockers, beta-blockers, potassium blockers, calcium blockers.

Class one blocks the sodium channel, so conduction slows and the QRS widens. Its three subclasses differ in one thing: how long the drug stays on the channel before it lets go.

Class one C, flecainide and propafenone, lets go slowly. It is still on the channel when the next beat arrives, so the QRS widens visibly at ordinary rates. And the faster the heart, the less time there is to let go, so the block deepens with rate. That is use dependence. The danger is the slowing itself: in a ventricle with a scar, slow conduction is one of the two ingredients of re-entry. In the CAST trial, flecainide given after infarction to suppress ectopic beats increased deaths. So class one C is for the structurally normal heart only.

Class one B, lidocaine and mexiletine, lets go in a fraction of a second. In healthy tissue it is gone before the next beat, so the ECG hardly changes. But it binds best to inactivated channels, and that is the state of a depolarised, ischaemic cell. So lidocaine picks out the sick ventricle and spares the rest. It is for the ventricular arrhythmias of ischaemia, and it is useless in the atria.

Class one A, quinidine, procainamide and disopyramide, sits in between, and also blocks potassium channels. So it widens the QRS and lengthens the QT, and its danger is torsades.

Class two is the beta-blockers. They lift the sympathetic hand: phase four flattens, the sinus rate falls, and the PR lengthens. They are the one class that reliably lowers sudden death after an infarct and in heart failure.

Class three blocks the potassium current of phase three. The action potential, the QT and the refractory period all lengthen, which is how these drugs stop a loop: the impulse comes round and finds the tissue still refractory. The price is the early afterdepolarisation and torsades. Sotalol, dofetilide and ibutilide are the clean examples, and they lengthen the QT most at slow rates, the reverse of class one. So their torsades appears during bradycardia and after pauses. Amiodarone is filed in class three but blocks sodium channels, beta receptors and calcium channels as well. It lengthens the QT, yet rarely causes torsades. Its price is paid in the thyroid, the lungs and the liver.

Class four is verapamil and diltiazem. They act where the upstroke is calcium, in the sinus and AV nodes: a slower rate, a longer PR, and no change in the QRS or the QT. They also weaken the ventricle.

{{**Vaughan Williams**
Class | Current | ECG
Ia quinidine, procainamide | Na + K | QRS ↑, QT ↑
Ib lidocaine, mexiletine | Na (fast off) | little change
Ic flecainide, propafenone | Na (slow off) | QRS ↑↑
II beta-blockers | phase 4, node | rate ↓, PR ↑
III amiodarone, sotalol | K | QT ↑
IV verapamil, diltiazem | Ca, node | rate ↓, PR ↑}}

[[Class one blocks sodium and widens the QRS. Class three blocks potassium and lengthens the QT. Classes two and four act on the calcium node: a slower rate and a longer PR.]]

Some drugs sit outside the scheme. Adenosine and atropine you know. Digoxin blocks the sodium-potassium pump, which strengthens contraction, and raises vagal tone, which slows the node. At ordinary doses it leaves a signature: a longer PR, a short QT, and an ST segment that sags like a scoop. That is the drug's effect, not toxicity. Magnesium quietens the calcium current behind early afterdepolarisations, which is why it treats torsades. And ivabradine blocks the funny current of phase four, so it slows the sinus node and nothing else, and is useless in atrial fibrillation. A modernised Oxford scheme of twenty eighteen gives it its own class, class zero. You need only the name.

[[Class one C drugs block more as the rate rises and are for structurally normal hearts only. Pure class three drugs lengthen the QT most at slow rates, so their torsades follows bradycardia and pauses.]]
lesson.cap: Class I blocks phase 0 (QRS; Ic most). II and IV slow the node (PR, rate). III blocks phase 3 (QT). Adenosine and digoxin act on the node.

steps.bridge: Each class had its own way of doing harm. The purest example of a drug for one tissue is adenosine.

lesson.text:
The same rhythm can need different drugs in two patients, because an antiarrhythmic is chosen by the heart it is going into. Every rule here is one drug's known danger meeting one heart's known weakness. Take the hearts one at a time.

The structurally normal heart with atrial fibrillation, when the aim is to restore sinus rhythm. Flecainide or propafenone. There is no scar for slowed conduction to exploit. But remember flutter: a class one C drug can organise the atria into a slow flutter that the node conducts one to one. So it is given with a drug that blocks the node.

The scarred or failing ventricle. Here class one C is forbidden, because of CAST. Verapamil and diltiazem are forbidden, because they weaken a weak pump. Dronedarone raises mortality in severe heart failure. What is left is amiodarone, which hardly depresses contraction. So amiodarone is the answer for atrial fibrillation in heart failure and for ventricular tachycardia from a scar, with lidocaine as the alternative when the ventricle is ischaemic.

The heart with an accessory pathway. Block the pathway, never the node: procainamide or ibutilide for pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

The heart with a long QT. The rule is not to add to it. Torsades from a drug or a low potassium is treated with magnesium, by stopping the drug, by lifting the potassium, and by raising the heart rate with pacing or isoprenaline, because a faster rate shortens the QT and removes the pauses. Amiodarone, sotalol and procainamide would lengthen it further. The inherited long QT is different in one way: its attacks are set off by adrenaline, by exertion, fright or sudden noise. So its long-term drug is a beta-blocker of the non-selective kind, nadolol or propranolol, and isoprenaline is avoided.

That patient also has to be put to sleep for surgery sometimes, and a grand test asked which agent is safe. The answer is propofol, which does not lengthen the QT and may shorten it. The inhaled agents, sevoflurane included, lengthen it. So do ondansetron and droperidol, the usual drugs for nausea. Ketamine and suxamethonium are avoided, and reversal with neostigmine and an anticholinergic lengthens the QT too. The principle is the same as on the ward: nothing that lengthens the QT, nothing that causes an adrenaline surge, and magnesium within reach.

[[In congenital long QT, propofol is the safe anaesthetic. Sevoflurane, ondansetron and droperidol lengthen the QT. The long-term drug is nadolol or propranolol.]]

The heart with Brugada syndrome. You met the notch of phase one, the brief outward potassium current that is strongest on the outer surface of the right ventricle. In Brugada syndrome the sodium current is weak, so that notch goes unopposed, and the result is the coved ST elevation in V1 and V2. Any sodium blocker weakens the sodium current further. So flecainide and procainamide bring out the pattern, which is how they are used as a test, and they are forbidden as treatment. Quinidine is the exception that proves the mechanism. It is a class one drug, but it also blocks that outward notch current, so it is the one drug used in Brugada syndrome. Fever unmasks the pattern too, so it is treated promptly.

And the heart you cannot classify. A wide regular tachycardia that might be supraventricular must not be given verapamil. If it is ventricular, as it usually is, the vessels dilate, the pump weakens and the patient collapses.

{{**Never**
Scar or heart failure | flecainide, verapamil, diltiazem, dronedarone
Pre-excited AF | adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blocker, digoxin, IV amiodarone
Long QT, torsades | amiodarone, sotalol, procainamide
Brugada | flecainide, procainamide
Wide tachycardia | verapamil}}

[[Flecainide only in a structurally normal heart. Amiodarone for the scarred or failing ventricle. Nodal blockers never in pre-excited fibrillation. Sodium blockers never in Brugada syndrome, except quinidine.]]

What these drugs do in overdose, and their antidotes, is the Cardiac drugs packet. Three short cards finish this section, beginning with the drug that acts on one tissue for ten seconds.

steps.bridge: Adenosine acts for seconds and tests the node. The drugs for a wide tachycardia are infused, each with a stopping rule.

lesson.text:
Adenosine is the cleanest example of a drug hung on one tissue. It opens the potassium channel of the nodal cell, the same one the vagus opens, and it is gone in under ten seconds. On the monitor you see its whole pharmacology: a few seconds in which no P wave conducts, and then the rhythm you started with, or sinus rhythm.

The card's numbers follow from the half-life. Six milligrams as a rapid push into a large vein, chased at once with a saline flush, because a slow injection is destroyed on the way.
