If that fails, twelve milligrams. Marrow asked exactly that: stable supraventricular tachycardia, six milligrams has failed, next step? Twelve. And the reduced first dose, three milligrams on the exam, when it arrives undiluted through a central line.

What it converts is any loop that includes the node: AVNRT, AVRT and some atrial tachycardias. What it only unmasks is everything else. The grand test gave six milligrams through a central line, a brief slowing, and sawtooth waves at three hundred a minute: atrial flutter with two to one conduction.

[[If adenosine stops the tachycardia, the node was in the loop. If it only slows it and the rhythm returns, the rhythm is atrial: look for flutter waves.]]

The adverse effect on the card is severe bronchospasm in asthma, so the asthmatic gets verapamil or diltiazem. Most patients also feel a flush, chest tightness and a few seconds of dread, so warn them.

One limit. When the tachycardia stops and returns within seconds, more adenosine buys another half minute and no more. In the item with an unstable child whose tachycardia kept returning, the answer was synchronised cardioversion.

steps.bridge: One sweep of true or false to close, and its last statement opens the next subject: what potassium does to the T wave.

lesson.text:
Three intravenous drugs for a stable wide tachycardia, and each stopping rule on this card is the drug's own class showing itself. Learn them that way and there is little left to memorise.

Procainamide is class one A: sodium block with some potassium block. It is infused until one of four things happens. The arrhythmia stops. The blood pressure falls. The QRS widens by more than half, which is the sodium block going too far. Or the ceiling dose is reached. And it is avoided with a long QT, which is the potassium block, and in heart failure.

Amiodarone is the drug for the weak ventricle: a loading dose over ten minutes, then an infusion. It has no bar on this card, which is exactly why it is the default when the heart is diseased.

Sotalol is a beta-blocker that is also a class three drug. It is avoided with a long QT. And it carries the one fact on this card that NEET has asked, in twenty twenty-four: the adverse effect of sotalol is due to what? Because it is a beta-blocker, the tempting options are bradycardia and hypotension. The answer is prolongation of the QT, from potassium channel block, and the torsades that follows. You could have worked that out from its class alone.

{{**Stable wide-QRS tachycardia, IV**
Procainamide | 20–50 mg/min; stop at suppression, hypotension, QRS +50% or 17 mg/kg; then 1–4 mg/min
Amiodarone | 150 mg over 10 min; then 1 mg/min for 6 h
Sotalol | 100 mg (1.5 mg/kg) over 5 min}}

[[Sotalol's serious adverse effect is QT prolongation and torsades, from potassium channel block. Procainamide is stopped when the QRS widens by half, and both are barred by a long QT.]]

The numbers themselves are on the screen and are drilled in the Rhythm packet. Say them once now. Procainamide at twenty to fifty milligrams a minute, to a ceiling of seventeen milligrams per kilogram. Amiodarone, one hundred and fifty milligrams over ten minutes, then one milligram a minute for six hours. Sotalol, one hundred milligrams over five minutes. The twenty twenty-five American algorithm lists only procainamide and amiodarone in its dose box. The guideline text still allows sotalol, and the card and the older keys list it, so do not mark sotalol as wrong.

steps.bridge: The drugs act through channels. The salts act on the same channels all day: next, potassium, calcium and magnesium.

lesson.text:
This card is a sweep of nine true or false statements from across cardiology. Four of them belong to what you have just built, so answer those from the mechanism and leave the rest to their own packets.

Adenosine is first line for supraventricular tachycardia in an asthmatic. False. It can provoke bronchospasm, so the node is closed with verapamil or diltiazem.

Verapamil is fine for rate control when the ejection fraction is thirty per cent. False. Class four drugs weaken a weak ventricle.

The maximum dose of atropine is three milligrams. True. At that dose the vagal hand is fully lifted.

Now look at the pattern in those. Each false statement takes a correct default and applies it to the heart that is the exception. Being stable allows you to use a drug. The airway, the ventricle and the accessory pathway still decide which one.

[[A stable patient may be given a drug, but the airway, the ventricle and the pathway choose it: no adenosine in asthma, no verapamil with a low ejection fraction, no nodal blocker in pre-excited fibrillation.]]

The fourth statement is the one that matters for where we go next. Peaked T waves are a sign of digoxin toxicity. False. Digoxin gives the scooped ST segment and a short QT, and in toxicity it gives ectopic beats together with block. A tall, narrow, peaked T wave is hyperkalaemia. The two are easy to confuse because they travel together: severe digoxin poisoning stops the sodium-potassium pump everywhere, so potassium rises, and then the peaked T does appear, but as the mark of the potassium, not of the drug.

The remaining statements you will meet in their own packets: no pulse check after a no shock advised message, angiography two to twenty-four hours after successful thrombolysis, veno-arterial and not veno-venous support during resuscitation, anticoagulation and not thrombolysis for a normotensive pulmonary embolism, and warfarin, not dabigatran, in rheumatic mitral stenosis with fibrillation.

So the drugs are hung on the action potential. But a drug is only an outside hand on a channel. The same channels answer all day long to the salts in the blood around them. Change the potassium, the calcium or the magnesium, and the waves change, each in the way you would now predict. That is next.

spine: The four classes are the four handles of the action potential: sodium, beta, potassium, calcium.
Class I widens the QRS (Ic most, Ib least, Ia adds a long QT); class III lengthens the QT; II and IV slow the node and lengthen PR.
Each drug's danger is its class: Ic kills in scarred ventricles (CAST); Ia and pure class III drugs cause torsades.
The heart chooses: flecainide for normal hearts, amiodarone for scar or failure, procainamide for a pathway, magnesium for torsades.
Never: verapamil for a wide tachycardia or low EF, nodal blockers in pre-excited AF, sodium blockers in Brugada, QT drugs in long QT.
Adenosine is the 10-second test of the node: it stops a nodal loop and unmasks an atrial one.

questions.text: What changes the waves I: potassium, calcium and magnesium

open.text:
Here is this section in one sentence: an electrolyte is a drug the body already contains, and it acts on the very same phase of the action potential as the drugs you have just classified. So a high potassium widens the QRS exactly as a sodium-channel blocker does, and a low potassium stretches repolarisation exactly as a class three drug does.

You hold the map already. QRS is sodium, ST is calcium, T is potassium, and the QT is the whole cell. In this section we change the fluid outside the cell and watch each wave answer. Potassium comes first, because it kills fastest and is asked most. Then calcium, which touches only the ST segment. Then magnesium, which hides behind the other two.

Listen for one trap throughout. A long QT is not one thing. A long ST with a normal T wave is calcium. A flat T with a U wave is potassium. The exam offers them as if they were the same.

We begin with why the resting cell cares about potassium at all.

steps.bridge: You have the two stages of high potassium. Your card now pins a potassium level to each.

lesson.text:
Start with a sentence that joins two things you learned apart. High potassium and a sodium-channel blocker draw the same wide, slurred QRS, because both leave the ventricle short of working sodium channels.

In the first ECG packet the resting cell sat at about minus ninety millivolts. What sets that number is potassium. At rest the membrane is open almost only to potassium, and potassium is about thirty times more concentrated inside than outside, so it leaks out and leaves the inside negative. Raise the potassium outside, the gradient flattens, less leaks out, and the cell rests at a less negative voltage: minus eighty, then minus seventy.

A high potassium has two effects, and they arrive in order.

The first is on repolarisation. The potassium channels that end the action potential, the ones that draw the T wave, have an odd property: they conduct better when there is more potassium outside. So phase three runs faster, and the T wave becomes tall, narrow, symmetrical and pointed, like a tent, with a short QT. The QRS is still normal.

The second effect is on the sodium channel, and this is the dangerous one. Think of a sodium channel as a camera flash. It fires once, then it must recharge, and it recharges only when the membrane returns all the way down to minus ninety. If the cell now rests at minus seventy, many channels never recharge. They sit inactivated, so with the next impulse fewer channels open, phase zero rises slowly, and conduction crawls.

Slow conduction, everywhere, is what you then read. The atria are the most sensitive, so the P wave flattens, widens and disappears, even though the sinus node is still firing and its impulse still reaches the AV node. A rhythm with no P waves that is still sinus is called sinoventricular rhythm. The PR lengthens. The QRS widens, the axis turns bizarre, and the ST can lift in V1 and V2 so that it imitates Brugada or an infarct. Finally the wide QRS merges with the tall T into a sine wave, and from there it is ventricular fibrillation, asystole or a slow pulseless rhythm.

[[High potassium acts twice. First it speeds phase three: a tall, narrow, tented T with a short QT. Then it inactivates sodium channels: the P wave vanishes, the PR and QRS widen, and the trace becomes a sine wave.]]

Low potassium is the mirror image on repolarisation. With less potassium outside, those same channels conduct poorly and phase three drags. The T wave flattens, the ST sags, and a U wave appears after the T and grows. A long, slow repolarisation is the soil for the early afterdepolarisations of the rhythm section, so the result is ectopics, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia and torsades. Low potassium also makes digoxin more toxic, and the last section explains why.

One warning. The ECG is a poor thermometer for potassium. Chronic kidney disease may carry seven with a near-normal trace, while a rapid rise, a low calcium or an acidosis makes the same level lethal. NEET's favourite wrong idea here is that a normal ECG makes a high potassium safe.

Last, why calcium works. It does nothing to the potassium level. Extra calcium outside the cell shifts the threshold of the sodium channels to a less negative voltage, which restores the gap between resting potential and threshold. It acts in one to three minutes and lasts half an hour to an hour.

[[Intravenous calcium does not lower potassium. It restores the gap between resting potential and threshold within minutes, so it is given for the ECG change, not for the number.]]

Next, your card puts potassium levels beside each of these stages.
lesson.cap: High potassium lifts the resting potential towards threshold. Calcium raises the threshold and restores the gap: it protects the heart but leaves potassium unchanged.

steps.bridge: The trace decides urgency. Now: what raises potassium in the ICU, and two questions you missed.

lesson.text:
Your card ties those stages to numbers, so this is only labelling.

Above about six millimoles per litre: the tall peaked T and the short QT. That is the faster phase three. Above about seven point five: the PR lengthens, the P wave flattens and the QRS widens. That is sodium channels dropping out, atria first. Above about nine: no P wave at all, and the sine wave. After that, ventricular standstill or fibrillation.

{{**Potassium (mmol/L) | ECG**
Over 6.0 | tall peaked T, short QT
Over 7.5 | long PR, flat P, wide QRS
Over 9.0 | no P, sine wave
Then | standstill or VF}}

Treat the numbers as a rough ladder, never as a promise. Stages can be skipped, and a patient can go from peaked T waves straight to arrest. So the card's own warning is the exam point: the ECG, not the number, decides urgency.

[[In hyperkalaemia any ECG change means calcium first, then shift the potassium, then remove it. The trace decides the urgency; the laboratory number does not.]]

One loop back. A wide QRS with no P waves and a slow rate looks like the complete heart block of the blocks section. Before you call it that, ask for the potassium. The bedside sign that goes with it is weakness climbing up the limbs, because skeletal muscle has the same inactivated sodium channels.

So where does a high potassium come from in the ICU?
lesson.cap: High potassium: peaked T → P flattens, PR lengthens → QRS widens → sine wave → VF or asystole. Stages can be skipped.

steps.bridge: High potassium done. Now the mirror image: the flat T and the U wave of low potassium.

lesson.text:
Only two things raise the serum potassium: potassium leaves the cells, or the kidney fails to excrete it. Ninety-eight per cent of the body's potassium is inside cells, so a small leak makes a big number.

Take the shift first. Acidosis pushes potassium out, and a mineral acidosis, such as that of renal failure, does it far more than lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis. Lack of insulin and a high osmolality do it too, and that explains the paradox of diabetic ketoacidosis: the serum potassium is high or normal while the body is deeply short of it. Give insulin and it falls fast. So you check the potassium before insulin, and if it is below three point five you replace potassium first. Older American keys put that line at three point three. Then cell death: rhabdomyolysis and crush, tumour lysis, haemolysis, old stored blood in a massive transfusion, and the washout when an ischaemic limb is reperfused. Two drugs shift it as well: beta-blockers a little, and digoxin in overdose, which blocks the pump that carries potassium into cells. Keep that for the last section.

Then suxamethonium, where you only need the mechanism. In a normal patient it opens the receptors at the motor end plate and the potassium rises by about half a millimole per litre. After denervation or long immobility the muscle spreads immature receptors over its whole surface. Now the same dose opens channels along the entire fibre and the potassium can rise by five to ten. The states are burns after the first day or two, spinal cord injury, stroke, Guillain-Barré syndrome, crush, and a long ICU stay.

Now reduced excretion. Acute and chronic kidney disease are obvious. The one the exam hides is a failure of aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the collecting duct secrete potassium and hydrogen ions. Remove it or block it, and both are retained: a high potassium with a normal anion gap acidosis.

[[A normal anion gap acidosis with a high potassium is type four renal tubular acidosis: too little aldosterone effect. Types one and two waste potassium, so their potassium is low.]]

That was a grand test question you missed. The typical patient is a diabetic with mild kidney disease and low renin. The drugs that do the same are ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim and heparin.

Before treating, exclude the false alarm. A haemolysed sample, a very high platelet count, or a clenched fist during sampling releases potassium in the tube. The clue is a normal ECG in a well patient. Repeat the sample.

Treatment belongs to your electrolyte deck, so one line: calcium to protect, insulin with glucose and salbutamol to shift, then binders, diuretics or dialysis to remove. But one dialysis detail was asked, and missed. End-stage kidney disease, potassium seven point two, peaked T waves and a widening QRS, emergency haemodialysis. What potassium should the dialysate contain? The options were zero, one, four and five.

[[For life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG change the keyed dialysate potassium is one millimole per litre. Not zero: too steep a fall in potassium is itself arrhythmogenic.]]

Four and five would remove almost nothing. Zero looks logical, and it is the trap. For routine dialysis in a stable patient the bath is higher, two or three, for the same reason.

Next, the opposite trace: your card for the low potassium.

steps.bridge: Potassium reshaped the T wave. Calcium leaves the T alone and changes the ST segment.

lesson.text:
Now run the film backwards. You have the mechanism: less potassium outside, slower phase three. Your card gives the order in which the trace changes.

First the T wave flattens. That is the earliest sign. Second, a U wave appears after it, best seen in V2 and V3. Third, the ST segment sinks and the U wave grows taller than the T. Fourth, T and U merge into one long hump, so the QT looks prolonged when it is really a QU interval, and the PR lengthens.

{{**Potassium (mmol/L) | ECG**
About 2.8 | flat T
About 2.5 | U wave
About 2.0 | U taller than T, ST depression
About 1.7 | T and U fused: long QU}}

Marrow adds a fifth step, and it is the one that matters: the long QU can break into torsades, ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation. That is why magnesium is replaced alongside potassium, and you will hear the reason three cards on.

The mimic is a high potassium read too quickly. Both can show a prominent wave after the QRS. In high potassium it is a tall narrow T with a short QT. In low potassium the T is flat and the tall wave is the U that follows it.

[[Low potassium: flat T first, then a U wave, then ST depression, then T and U fused into a long QU, then torsades. A tall wave after a flat T is a U wave, not a peaked T.]]

Potassium changed the T wave. The next ion leaves the T alone and changes the segment before it.
lesson.cap: Low potassium: ST depression, flat T, prominent U (U taller than T when severe), apparent long QT (really QU).

steps.bridge: Low calcium stretched the ST. Now the reverse: high calcium and the short QT.

lesson.text:
Remember the line from the first ECG packet: QRS is sodium, ST is calcium, T is potassium. Here is the calcium part made real.

The ST segment is the plateau, phase two, and the plateau is calcium flowing in through the L-type channel. That channel is partly shut by the very calcium that has entered. When calcium is low, less comes in, the channel takes longer to shut, and the plateau lasts longer. So the ST segment lengthens. The T wave that follows is normal in shape and size, because the potassium channels are untouched.

[[Low calcium gives a long QT by stretching the ST segment, with a normal T wave. Low potassium and the QT drugs give a long QT by stretching and flattening the T. Same interval, different part.]]

Torsades is uncommon with a low calcium alone, which fits: repolarisation itself is even. Your card adds bradycardia, hypotension and heart failure, because calcium is also the trigger for contraction, and it puts the danger zone at an ionised calcium below zero point six five millimoles per litre.

The card's other half is nerve and muscle: tingling round the mouth and in the fingers, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, seizures, Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign. Trousseau, the hand spasm with a cuff held above systolic pressure for three minutes, is the more specific.

Where will you meet it? A low ionised calcium is found in more than half of ICU patients. The makers are citrate, from a massive transfusion or from the anticoagulation of a filter circuit; pancreatitis; the early phase of rhabdomyolysis; sepsis; a low magnesium; the hungry bones after parathyroid surgery; and alkalosis, which makes albumin bind more calcium, so the ionised fraction falls while the total stays the same.

One question you missed lives here. A patient on digoxin has symptomatic hypocalcaemia. The tempting answer is to withhold calcium, from the old fear that calcium and digoxin together stop the heart. The key was intravenous calcium gluconate, given slowly with ECG monitoring, and correction of the magnesium.

Now raise the calcium instead.
lesson.cap: Calcium moves only the ST: low calcium = long ST and long QT with a normal T; high calcium = short ST and short QT.

steps.bridge: Two ions down. Magnesium is why low potassium and low calcium sometimes refuse to correct.

lesson.text:
High calcium is the exact reverse. More calcium rushes in, the L-type channel shuts sooner, and the plateau is cut short. The ST segment shrinks until the T wave seems to rise straight out of the QRS. So the QT is short.

At very high levels three more things appear. A J wave, the same notch at the end of the QRS that you will meet in hypothermia as the Osborn wave, here at a normal temperature. A wider QRS. And slowing of the nodes, with bradycardia and AV block, which can end in arrest. It also makes digoxin more toxic, since digoxin works by loading the cell with calcium.

[[Calcium and the QT move in opposite directions. High calcium: short ST, short QT. Low calcium: long ST, long QT. In both the T wave keeps its shape.]]

DocT asked two things. The trap of calling the QT long in hypercalcaemia. And a stem with Osborn waves at a normal temperature, a short QT and hilar nodes on both sides: sarcoidosis, where the granulomas make active vitamin D.

The rest of your card is the body: weakness, a clouded mind, constipation, and polyuria, which dries the patient out and raises the calcium further. That is why saline comes first.

One grand test question you skipped: calcium fifteen, kidney failure, and an ejection fraction of thirty per cent. Saline needs a kidney to excrete it and a heart to tolerate it. This patient has neither, so the answer was haemodialysis.

Two ions down. The third is the reason the other two sometimes refuse to correct.
lesson.cap: Calcium moves only the ST: low calcium = long ST and long QT with a normal T; high calcium = short ST and short QT.

steps.bridge: Too little magnesium gives torsades. Too much gives heart block: the ladder is next.

lesson.text:
Magnesium is the ion you treat without seeing it on the trace. Its ECG signs are mostly borrowed: they are the signs of the potassium and the calcium that it drags down with it.

Magnesium has three jobs here. It is the cofactor of the sodium-potassium pump. Inside the kidney cell it plugs the channel through which the collecting duct secretes potassium. And it is needed for parathyroid hormone to be released and to act.

So when magnesium is low, three things follow. The pump falters. The plug comes out, and the kidney pours potassium into the urine however much you infuse. And parathyroid hormone fails, so the calcium falls. That is your card's line: refractory hypokalaemia and refractory hypocalcaemia.

[[A low potassium that will not correct means a low magnesium. Without magnesium the kidney's potassium channel stays open and the infused potassium is lost in the urine. Replace both together.]]

The ECG is therefore a mixture. A long QT and U waves from the potassium, ST depression, and on your card a wider QRS and peaked T waves. What matters is the rhythm: ectopics, torsades, ventricular fibrillation, and more digoxin toxicity. Outside the heart the card lists tetany, seizures, and nystagmus in both the horizontal and the vertical direction.

Now the question you skipped. Septic shock, potassium two point four, magnesium one point two, calcium seven point six, ventricular ectopics, a central line and no gut route. Four plans were offered. Potassium in dextrose: wrong, because dextrose releases insulin and drives potassium into cells, so the carrier is saline. Potassium at fifty millimoles an hour: too fast; twenty an hour through a central line with monitoring is the working ceiling. Waiting for the magnesium to be normal before giving potassium: wrong, the ectopy cannot wait. The key was potassium in saline at twenty an hour, together with magnesium.

And remember the other use. In torsades, magnesium two grams is given even when the serum level is normal, because there it is acting as a drug that suppresses the afterdepolarisation, not as a replacement.

Give too much of it and you get the last card of this section.

steps.bridge: Three ions done, and the QT stretched twice. Next section: the QT itself.

lesson.text:
Your card says magnesium is a natural calcium antagonist, and that sentence predicts the whole picture. Think of a slow overdose of verapamil, with a weakened nerve to muscle junction added.

As the level climbs, the knee jerk goes first. Then the PR lengthens and the QRS widens. Then complete heart block, then arrest, with hypotension, flushing and weak breathing along the way.

{{**Magnesium (mEq/L) | Sign**
Over 4 | reflexes reduced
Over 5 | first-degree AV block
Over 10 | complete heart block
Over 13 | cardiac arrest
1 mEq/L = 0.5 mmol/L = 1.2 mg/dL}}

A caution about units. This ladder comes from Marino's textbook and is in milliequivalents per litre. Your card's heading says millimoles, and that is a slip: in millimoles each figure would be half. Obstetric texts quote somewhat higher levels, so learn the order and not the decimals.

[[Rising magnesium: knee jerk lost, then a long PR, then complete heart block, then arrest. The antidote is calcium, and the knee jerk is checked before every dose.]]

It happens in two patients: the woman on a magnesium infusion for eclampsia, and the patient with renal failure given magnesium antacids or laxatives. Calcium gluconate reverses it for minutes, and dialysis removes it.

That finishes the three ions. Twice in this section the QT stretched. The next section takes the QT on its own.

spine: Potassium sets the resting potential. High K⁺: first faster phase 3 (tented T, short QT), then inactivated Na⁺ channels (no P, long PR, wide QRS, sine wave).
The ECG, not the number, sets urgency. Calcium restores the resting-to-threshold gap in minutes and does not lower K⁺.
High K⁺ = shift out of cells or failed excretion. NAGMA + high K⁺ = type 4 RTA. Emergency dialysate K⁺ = 1 mmol/L, never 0.
Low K⁺: flat T → U wave → ST depression → fused T-U (long QU) → torsades.
Calcium acts on the ST only: low Ca²⁺ = long ST, long QT, normal T; high Ca²⁺ = short QT, J wave when very high.
Low Mg²⁺ hides behind refractory low K⁺ and low Ca²⁺ and gives torsades: replace both. High Mg²⁺: knee jerk lost → long PR → complete block → arrest.

questions.text: The QT: what it measures, what stretches it, and torsades

open.text:
A long QT and a wide QRS are not two grades of the same problem. A wide QRS is slow conduction, a sodium problem, and its danger is re-entry. A long QT is slow recovery, a potassium problem, and its danger is a triggered beat that falls on a half-recovered ventricle. Different channel, different rhythm, different drug.

You have now seen the QT stretch three times: with a low potassium, with a low calcium, and with the class one A and class three drugs. This section puts the QT in the centre. First how to measure it honestly, because a QT read without the heart rate means nothing. Then the people born with a long QT: three channels, three triggers, and the score a grand test asked you to add up. Then the drugs and illnesses that lengthen it in the ICU. And then what it leads to: torsades de pointes, where the early afterdepolarisation of the rhythm section finally becomes a rhythm.

The trap to listen for is treating torsades like ordinary ventricular tachycardia. The drug that cures one feeds the other.

steps.bridge: You can measure and correct a QT. Now the people born with a long one, and the Schwartz score.

lesson.text:
The QT interval is the action potential of the ventricle seen from outside: from the first sodium channel opening to the last potassium channel closing. So you measure from the very start of the QRS to the end of the T wave.

Three practical rules. Use the lead where the QT is longest and the T wave ends cleanly, usually lead two or V5. Find the end of the T by drawing a line down its steepest falling slope; where that line meets the baseline is the end. This is the tangent method. And leave the U wave out.

Now the correction. The action potential shortens when the heart beats faster. That is normal, and without it there would be no time for diastole at a rate of one hundred and fifty. So a raw QT of four hundred milliseconds is long at a rate of one hundred and short at a rate of fifty. To compare patients you convert it to what it would be at sixty beats a minute. That is the corrected QT, the QTc.

The usual formula is Bazett's: the QT divided by the square root of the R to R interval in seconds. At a rate of sixty the R to R interval is one second, the square root of one is one, and the QT and the QTc are equal. Bazett has one fault, and it is a classic question. It overcorrects at fast rates, so it calls a normal QT long during a tachycardia, and it undercorrects at slow rates. Fridericia's formula, which uses the cube root, and the Framingham formula, which is linear, behave better at the extremes.

[[Bazett: the QTc is the QT divided by the square root of the R to R interval in seconds. It overcorrects at fast heart rates and undercorrects at slow ones; Fridericia's cube root is better at the extremes.]]

A bedside shortcut for rates between sixty and a hundred: the T wave should end before the halfway point between two R waves. If it crosses halfway, measure properly.

One more correction. The QT contains the QRS. In a bundle branch block or a paced rhythm the QRS is wide, so the QT is long with no fault of repolarisation. There you use the JT interval, from the end of the QRS to the end of the T, or subtract the extra QRS width.

Now the numbers.

{{**QTc | Meaning**
Up to 450 ms men, 460 ms women | normal
Over 500 ms, or a rise over 60 ms | high torsades risk
Under about 340 to 360 ms | short QT}}

The upper limit is four hundred and fifty milliseconds in men and four hundred and sixty in women. Your poisoning card uses a single older figure, four hundred and forty, so recognise both. Danger begins above five hundred, or when a drug has added more than sixty to the patient's own baseline. At that point the QT drugs are stopped and the potassium and magnesium corrected.

[[A QTc above five hundred milliseconds, or a rise of more than sixty from baseline, is the line for torsades risk. Stop the QT-prolonging drugs and correct potassium and magnesium.]]

The short QT is rare: below about three hundred and forty to three hundred and sixty. You know its common causes already, a high calcium and digoxin. Fever and an inherited short QT syndrome complete the list.

So who has a long QT? Some people are born with one.
lesson.cap: QT from QRS onset to the T end by the tangent method; leave out the U. Bazett QTc = QT/√RR overcorrects at fast rates.

steps.bridge: Inherited long QT is rare. The long QT you will meet in the ICU is acquired.

lesson.text:
Congenital long QT is three diseases sharing one ECG finding, and the way to tell them apart is to ask what the patient was doing when he collapsed.

Go back to phase three. Two potassium currents repolarise the ventricle, a slow one and a rapid one. And the sodium channel that opened in phase zero must stay shut through the plateau. Break any of the three and the action potential lengthens.

Type one is loss of the slow potassium current. The gene is KCNQ1. This current is the reserve that sympathetic drive switches on to shorten the action potential during exercise. Without it the QT fails to shorten as the rate climbs. So events come with exertion, and swimming is the classic trigger. The T wave is broad-based. Beta-blockers work best here.

Type two is loss of the rapid potassium current. The gene is KCNH2 and the channel is called hERG, the channel that nearly every QT-prolonging drug blocks. Events come with a sudden noise, an alarm clock or a telephone, with emotion, and in the months after childbirth. The T wave is low and notched.

Type three is different in kind. The gene is SCN5A, the cardiac sodium channel, and the fault is a gain of function: a late sodium current leaks in through the plateau. Events come at rest and in sleep, when the heart is slow. The ST segment is long and flat with a late, peaked T. Mexiletine, a class one B drug that blocks this late current, helps. Notice the gene. Loss of function in the same gene is Brugada syndrome, which closes this section.

{{**Type | Gene, current | Trigger | T wave**
LQT1 | KCNQ1, slow K⁺ lost | exercise, swimming | broad
LQT2 | KCNH2 (hERG), rapid K⁺ lost | noise, emotion, postpartum | notched, low
LQT3 | SCN5A, late Na⁺ gained | sleep, rest | long ST, late T}}

[[Long QT one: exercise and swimming. Long QT two: sudden noise and the postpartum period. Long QT three: sleep. One and two are lost potassium currents; three is a sodium channel that leaks.]]

Two names for inheritance. Romano-Ward is autosomal dominant, with normal hearing, and is nearly every case. Jervell and Lange-Nielsen is autosomal recessive, with congenital sensorineural deafness, and is severe.

Now the Schwartz score, which a grand test asked you to calculate and you skipped. It adds ECG findings, history and family.

{{**Schwartz score**
QTc ≥480 = **3**; 460–479 = **2**; 450–459 (men) = 1
QTc ≥480 at 4th min of exercise recovery = 1
Torsades = **2**; T alternans = 1; notched T in 3 leads = 1; slow rate for age = 0.5
Syncope with stress = **2**; without = 1; deafness = 0.5
Relative with LQTS = 1; sudden death under 30 in family = 0.5
≤1 low; 1.5–3 intermediate; **≥3.5 high**}}

You do not need every half point. You need the three big ones: a QTc of four hundred and eighty or more scores three, syncope with stress scores two, and torsades scores two. Three and a half or more is a high probability.

Now the question. A swimmer who faints in the water, a QTc of four hundred and eighty-five, and a family history. The QTc gives three. Syncope with stress gives two. That is five already, and high. A relative with definite long QT adds one, and an unexplained sudden death before thirty in the immediate family adds a half, provided they are two different relatives. The total is six point five, which was the key. Be careful with the family part. If a stem gives only a sudden death in the family, with no relative proven to have long QT, the strict sum is five point five. Choose five point five if it is offered, and six point five if it is not. Either way the probability is high. Two rules stop you over-counting: syncope and torsades are not both scored, and one relative cannot earn both family points.

Treatment in one breath, because the rhythm packet repeats it. A non-selective beta-blocker, nadolol or propranolol, for everyone. No QT-prolonging drugs. Potassium and magnesium kept normal. An ICD after a cardiac arrest, or when events continue despite the beta-blocker, with left cardiac sympathetic denervation as a further step.

Most long QT in the ICU, though, is not inherited. It is given.
lesson.cap: LQT1 (KCNQ1): broad T, exercise and swimming. LQT2 (hERG): notched T, sudden noise, postpartum. LQT3 (SCN5A): long flat ST, late T, sleep.

steps.bridge: The QT is long. Next: the rhythm it leads to, torsades de pointes.

lesson.text:
Almost every drug that lengthens the QT does it through one door: the hERG channel, the rapid potassium current of phase three. That is the channel missing in congenital long QT type two. So an acquired long QT is a borrowed type two, and it behaves the same way: worse with a slow heart, worse after a pause, worse when the potassium is low.

Why that one channel? Its inner cavity is unusually wide and lined with residues that hold on to many unrelated molecules. That is why drugs from completely different families share this one side effect.

You do not need the full list. You need the families, and a name or two in each.

{{**QT-prolonging drugs**
Antiarrhythmics: class Ia, class III
Antimicrobials: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azoles, chloroquine, quinine
Psychiatric: haloperidol IV, droperidol, ziprasidone, quetiapine, citalopram, TCAs
Antiemetics: ondansetron, domperidone
Others: methadone, arsenic trioxide, volatile anaesthetics}}

The antiarrhythmics of class one A and class three, where it is the intended action. The antimicrobials: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, the azole antifungals and the antimalarials. The psychiatric drugs: haloperidol, especially intravenous, droperidol, ziprasidone, quetiapine, citalopram and the tricyclics. The antiemetics: ondansetron and domperidone. And a mixed group: methadone, the volatile anaesthetics, and arsenic trioxide, which is why the arsenic stem in your grand test carried a long QTc.

A drug rarely does it alone. Torsades needs the drug and a vulnerable patient. The states that add to the drug are a low potassium, a low magnesium, a low calcium, bradycardia and pauses, female sex, a diseased ventricle, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, liver failure, starvation, and a brain injury such as subarachnoid haemorrhage. When several QT drugs run together, the one to stop first is the one that also blocks the liver enzyme clearing the others, such as erythromycin or fluconazole.

[[Acquired long QT is a blocked hERG channel in a vulnerable patient: low potassium, low magnesium, a slow heart, female sex. Stop the drug, correct the ions and keep the rate up.]]

Two grand test misses sit here.

The first is organophosphate poisoning with a QTc of four hundred and seventy. What does it mean? You chose that it predicts atropine resistance. The other tempting answer is that it confirms severe poisoning. The key was the cautious one: it may indicate increased severity. In the studies, patients with a long QTc had more respiratory failure and a higher mortality, about one in three against one in twenty-five in one series. But that is an association, not a proof. When one option says confirms and another says may indicate, the modest one is usually right.

The second is the patient with congenital long QT who needs a general anaesthetic. Which agent is safe? The key was propofol, which does not lengthen the QT and may shorten it. The volatile agents, sevoflurane included, lengthen the QTc, so a total intravenous technique is the preferred answer, even though volatiles have often been used without harm. The other drugs to avoid follow from this lesson and the last one. Ondansetron and droperidol block hERG. Ketamine and adrenaline are sympathetic triggers. Suxamethonium, and reversal with neostigmine and an anticholinergic, disturb the rate and the QT. Keep the beta-blocker going, keep the ions normal, and blunt the surges at intubation and on waking.

[[Congenital long QT under anaesthesia: propofol is the safe agent. Sevoflurane and the other volatiles prolong the QTc; ondansetron, droperidol and ketamine are avoided; the beta-blocker is continued.]]

So the QT is long. What happens next is the subject of the next card.

steps.bridge: Torsades on your own card next, with a second channel disease beside it: Brugada.

lesson.text:
Here the early afterdepolarisation of the rhythm section finally becomes a rhythm.

First the wider family. In polymorphic ventricular tachycardia the QRS changes from beat to beat in height, axis and width, because activation takes a different path each time. Your card calls it multiple ventricular foci. Its commonest cause is not a long QT at all. It is ischaemia or infarction, with a normal QT.

Torsades de pointes is the special member: polymorphic VT that arises on a long QT. The name means twisting of the points, because the peaks of the complexes swing above the baseline and then below it, in a slow spindle.

How does it start? When repolarisation is long, calcium channels have time to recover during the plateau and reopen, and the membrane makes a small second upstroke before it has finished recovering. That is the early afterdepolarisation. If it reaches threshold it fires an extra beat, and that beat lands on the T wave of the beat before, the vulnerable period, when some muscle has recovered and some has not. The impulse threads through the recovered parts, and its path keeps shifting as other parts recover. Hence the twisting.

It is pause-dependent, and that explains the treatment. A pause makes the next action potential even longer. So the classic onset is short, long, short: an ectopic beat, a pause, a sinus beat with a huge QT, and then the beat that starts the run.

[[Torsades is polymorphic VT on a long QT, started by an early afterdepolarisation after a pause. So the treatment is magnesium, a faster heart rate, and removal of whatever lengthened the QT.]]

Magnesium, two grams intravenously, suppresses the afterdepolarisation without shortening the QT, and it can be repeated. Stop the offending drugs. Bring the potassium to the upper part of normal. If torsades keeps returning, raise the rate with overdrive pacing or isoprenaline, because a faster heart has a shorter QT and no pauses. And never amiodarone, sotalol or procainamide, which lengthen the QT further.

Now the shock, the last line of your card. A synchronised shock needs a constant R wave to time itself on. Here there is none, so the machine may not fire, or may fire on a T wave. Sustained polymorphic VT is therefore defibrillated: an unsynchronised shock at high energy. The arrest packet returns to this.

Keep one mimic. Polymorphic VT with a long QT on the sinus beats is torsades: magnesium. Polymorphic VT with a normal QT is ischaemia: treat the artery, and amiodarone or lidocaine are allowed. NEET's favourite wrong option is amiodarone for torsades.

The last card of the section has torsades in its first half and a new disease in its second.
lesson.cap: Torsades: long QT, short–long–short onset, QRS twisting around the baseline. Magnesium 2 g, raise the rate, stop QT drugs.

steps.bridge: Brugada is a weak sodium channel from birth. Next section: the sodium channel poisoned.

lesson.text:
Your card puts two diseases side by side, and they make a perfect pair for this packet. In both the echo is normal and the fault is in a channel. One is a disease of phase three. The other is a disease of phases zero and one.

The first half you have just heard, so check yourself against the card. Torsades: magnesium two grams, pacing or isoprenaline if it recurs, defibrillation if pulseless. Avoid amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol, because each lengthens the QT. One extension from Marrow: when the long QT has a removable cause, a drug or an electrolyte, you remove the cause and the patient does not need an ICD.

Now Brugada syndrome. The gene is SCN5A, the cardiac sodium channel, and this time it is a loss of function. Earlier in this section the same gene, with a gain of function, was long QT type three. One channel, two diseases, depending on whether it leaks or fails.

Why should a weak sodium current draw anything on the ECG? Go back to phase one, the small notch after the upstroke, made by a brief outward potassium current. It is deepest in the epicardium of the right ventricular outflow tract. Normally the sodium current before it and the calcium current after it overcome the notch, and the plateau follows. Weaken the sodium current, and in those epicardial cells the notch wins: the plateau, the dome, is lost. The endocardial cells beneath keep theirs. So during the ST segment there is a voltage difference across the wall of the right ventricular outflow tract, and the cameras sitting right over it are V1 and V2.

What they record is the type one pattern. The ST segment starts high, at least two millimetres above the baseline, and slopes down in a curve, coved like a shark's fin, into a negative T wave. It may show only when V1 and V2 are moved up one or two spaces, to the third or second intercostal space, directly over the outflow tract.

[[Brugada type one: coved ST elevation of at least two millimetres running down into a negative T wave in V1 or V2. The gene is SCN5A with loss of function. A saddle-back ST with a positive T is not diagnostic.]]

That negative T was a mini test question, and only fifty-seven per cent knew it.

Anything that removes more sodium current brings the pattern out or triggers the arrhythmia. Fever, because the faulty channels fail faster when warm. High vagal tone, so deaths come at rest and in sleep, typically in young men. And drugs: the class one sodium blockers, which is why ajmaline, flecainide or procainamide serve as a provocation test, and also tricyclics, lithium, cocaine, and propofol in prolonged infusion. A high potassium or a tricyclic overdose can draw the same shape in a normal heart; that is called a Brugada phenocopy.

Now the grand test question you left blank. A man of thirty-four survives a cardiac arrest at night, with a normal heart on echo and a coved ST in V1 to V3. What gives the greatest reduction in sudden death? The options were quinidine, a procainamide challenge, epicardial ablation and an ICD. The defect is permanent, the rhythm it causes is ventricular fibrillation, and no drug has been shown to prevent death. So he must carry the shock with him.

[[Brugada after a survived arrest: an ICD, class one. Quinidine, which blocks the outward current of the notch, is the adjunct for repeated shocks or a refused device; isoprenaline is for an electrical storm; fever is always treated.]]

Keep one contrast. Brugada kills at rest and has an abnormal resting ECG. Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT kills on exertion and has a normal resting ECG.

Brugada is what a weak sodium channel looks like from birth. The next section is what it looks like after an overdose.
lesson.cap: Brugada type 1: coved ST ≥ 2 mm into a negative T in V1–V2 (diagnostic). Type 2 saddleback is suggestive only. Unmasked by fever and sodium blockers.

spine: QT = QRS onset to T end (tangent, lead II or V5). Bazett QTc = QT/√RR: overcorrects fast, undercorrects slow. Normal ≤450 men, ≤460 women.
QTc >500 ms or a rise >60 ms = torsades risk: stop QT drugs, correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Congenital: LQT1 (KCNQ1, swimming), LQT2 (hERG, noise, postpartum), LQT3 (SCN5A gain, sleep). Schwartz ≥3.5 = high probability.
Acquired long QT = hERG block + a vulnerable patient (low K⁺, low Mg²⁺, bradycardia, female). LQTS anaesthesia: propofol.
Long QT → EAD after a pause → torsades: magnesium 2 g, raise the rate, stop the drug; never amiodarone. Sustained: unsynchronised shock.
Brugada = SCN5A loss: coved ST ≥2 mm + negative T in V1–V2; fever, sleep, Na⁺ blockers; survived arrest → ICD.

questions.text: Poisons that write on the ECG: sodium channels, digoxin and the node blockers

open.text:
A poison has no new way to change an ECG. It can only press on a channel you already know, harder than a doctor would. So an overdose is a Vaughan Williams class given in excess: a tricyclic is a class one drug, a beta-blocker is class two taken too far, verapamil is class four, and digoxin is the node slowed and the muscle irritated at once.

That means you can read the poison from the trace. A wide QRS with a tall R wave in aVR is the sodium channel. A long QT is the potassium channel. A slow rate with a long PR is the node. And a slow rhythm with ectopic beats breaking through it is digoxin.

This section holds more of your missed grand test questions than any other, so each is taught where it belongs. The doses and the order of the antidotes come later, in the cardiac drugs packet. Here you learn why each antidote fits its channel, which is what makes the doses easy to keep.

The trap to listen for is treating a poisoned wide-complex tachycardia with an ordinary antiarrhythmic. We start with the sodium channel, straight from the Brugada pattern you have just seen.

steps.bridge: Wide QRS means sodium and bicarbonate. Your card now sets all three poison pictures side by side.

lesson.text:
A tricyclic overdose is a class one antiarrhythmic poured over the whole heart at once. Everything on the ECG follows from one fact: the fast sodium channels of phase zero are blocked.

Block phase zero and conduction slows, so the QRS widens. That much you know. Now the detail that makes the pattern recognisable. The right bundle branch, long and thin, suffers most. So the last part of the heart to be activated is the right ventricle, late and unopposed, and the final forty milliseconds of the QRS point to the right and upward.

Which camera sits to the right and above? aVR, on the right shoulder. Normally everything in aVR is negative. In sodium-channel poisoning its QRS ends with a tall R wave. Lead one and aVL, on the opposite side, end with a deep slurred S wave.

{{**Sodium-channel blockade on the ECG**
QRS over 100 ms
Terminal R in aVR over 3 mm; R/S in aVR over 0.7
Deep slurred S in I and aVL
Sinus tachycardia; long QT; Brugada-like V1–V2}}

The rest of the tricyclic picture comes from its other actions. It is anticholinergic and blocks noradrenaline reuptake, so there is a sinus tachycardia with dilated pupils, dry skin and a full bladder. It blocks alpha receptors and depresses the muscle, so the pressure falls. It blocks potassium channels a little, so the QT is long. A fast sinus rhythm with a very wide QRS can be impossible to tell from ventricular tachycardia, and in an overdose both get the same first treatment.

Now the numbers. In nineteen eighty-five Boehnert and Lovejoy found that the drug level did not predict who got into trouble. The QRS did. About a third of patients at a hundred milliseconds or more had seizures, and about half of those at a hundred and sixty or more had ventricular arrhythmias.

[[Tricyclic overdose: a QRS of one hundred milliseconds or more predicts seizures, and one hundred and sixty or more predicts ventricular arrhythmia. A terminal R wave in aVR of three millimetres or more carries the same warning.]]

Why sodium bicarbonate works is the heart of this card, and it works twice. The sodium load raises the gradient and pushes more current through the channels still open. And the alkalosis changes the drug: at a higher pH less of it is in the charged form that binds inside the channel, so it lets go. It is given for a QRS above one hundred milliseconds, a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension, in boluses of one to two millimoles per kilogram until the QRS narrows, aiming for a pH of seven point four five to seven point five five.

The forbidden drugs are logical. Class one A and one C add to the block, and class three lengthens the QT. Physostigmine has caused asystole. Phenytoin is itself a sodium blocker, so seizures get a benzodiazepine. Lidocaine, the class one B drug that binds and leaves quickly, is the one antiarrhythmic allowed if bicarbonate fails.

[[A wide QRS from any sodium-channel poison gets sodium bicarbonate, one to two millimoles per kilogram, to a pH of about seven point five. Never a class one A or one C drug, never physostigmine, never phenytoin.]]

A grand test asked the threshold in a child, and you skipped it. It is the same figure: one hundred milliseconds. A child's normal QRS is narrower, so a hundred is already clearly wide. The sign that weakens in small children is the R wave in aVR, because the young right-dominant heart can show one normally.

And it is not only tricyclics. The same trace and the same antidote belong to cocaine, propranolol, flecainide and the class one A drugs, diphenhydramine, carbamazepine, quinine, chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine. Two of those were grand test questions. Cocaine with a wide QRS tachycardia: bicarbonate, where you chose verapamil. Propranolol with a QRS of one hundred and sixty: bicarbonate, because propranolol is the beta-blocker with membrane-stabilising action. Local anaesthetics belong to the family too, with lipid emulsion as their extra antidote.

Your own card now puts all three poison pictures on one page.
lesson.cap: Sodium-channel poisoning: sinus tachycardia, QRS ≥ 100 ms, terminal R in aVR ≥ 3 mm. QRS ≥ 100 ms → seizures; ≥ 160 ms → ventricular arrhythmia.

steps.bridge: Wide, long, slow. Digoxin is the odd one: slow and fast at once.

lesson.text:
Your card is the summary of the idea that opened this section: read the poison from the trace. Three pictures, three channels.

{{**ECG change | Channel | Think of**
Wide QRS, tall R in aVR | sodium | tricyclic, cocaine, carbamazepine, propranolol
Long QT | potassium (hERG) | antipsychotics, citalopram, macrolides, azoles, sotalol, ondansetron
Slow rate, AV block | the nodes | beta-blocker, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin}}

The wide QRS you have just done. Two details from the card. The normal QRS is under one hundred and twenty milliseconds, but in poisoning you act at one hundred. And the danger the card names is ventricular tachycardia, because slow, uneven conduction is the ground for re-entry, exactly as in the scarred ventricle of the rhythm section.

The bank has asked this card fifteen times, and most of the questions are one idea in different clothes: in a tricyclic overdose the ECG is the first test and the QRS is the risk score. A drowsy patient after amitriptyline, pulse one hundred and forty, pupils dilated. The first action among charcoal, a CT, an ECG and atenolol is the ECG. Charcoal is unsafe with an unprotected airway. What best stratifies risk seven hours after the overdose? The QRS duration, not the dose and not the level. Seizures, a wide-complex tachycardia, a QRS of one hundred and seventy-five and a full bladder: bicarbonate, not physostigmine. And massive propranolol, still in shock after glucagon, with a QRS of one hundred and eighty: bicarbonate again, because glucagon, insulin and calcium do not touch a conduction defect.

[[In poisoning a wide QRS means the sodium channel and bicarbonate. A long QT means the potassium channel: stop the drug and give magnesium and potassium. A slow rate means the nodes.]]

The second picture, the long QT, you built in the last section. The card's limit for the QTc is four hundred and forty. The facts asked: citalopram and escitalopram are the SSRIs that lengthen it. Typical and atypical antipsychotics carry about the same risk of arrhythmia, with thioridazine and ziprasidone lengthening the QT most. And sotalol is the beta-blocker that causes torsades.

The mimic to fix is wide against long. A wide QRS is conduction, and the answer is bicarbonate. A long QT is repolarisation, and the answer is magnesium. Some drugs do both, and a tricyclic is one, but the antidote follows the abnormality in front of you.

The third picture is the slow one. The card lists beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, cholinergic poisons, opioids, lithium and magnesium. We take digoxin first, because it is the only one that is slow and fast at once.

steps.bridge: Digoxin slows the node and irritates the muscle. Beta-blockers and calcium blockers only slow.

lesson.text:
Digoxin is the one drug that slows the node and excites the muscle in the same heart, and both actions come from a single blocked pump.

Digoxin blocks the sodium-potassium pump, so sodium builds up inside the cell. The cell normally expels calcium through an exchanger driven by sodium running in. With sodium already high inside, the exchanger slows and calcium stays in. More calcium means a stronger beat, which is the purpose of the drug. Separately, digoxin raises vagal tone, which slows the sinus node and the AV node, the calcium cells of the first packet.

At a therapeutic dose the ECG shows this as digoxin effect. The extra calcium shortens the plateau, so the QT is short. The ST segment sags in a smooth scoop in the lateral leads, the reverse tick, with a flat or inverted T. And the PR is a little long from the vagal action. None of this is toxicity. It only says the patient is taking the drug.

[[The scooped ST, the short QT and the slightly long PR are digoxin effect, not toxicity. Toxicity is diagnosed from rhythms. A peaked T wave is never digoxin: it is hyperkalaemia.]]

Toxicity is the same two actions taken too far. A cell overloaded with calcium leaks it from its stores after each beat, and that leak drives a small depolarisation after the action potential has finished: the delayed afterdepolarisation of the rhythm section. So irritable foci fire in atrium, junction and ventricle, while the vagal action blocks the node. Put the two together.

{{**Digoxin toxicity rhythms**
Ventricular ectopics, bigeminy (commonest)
Atrial tachycardia with block
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Regularised AF = complete block, junctional escape
Bidirectional VT
Sinus bradycardia, any AV block}}

Ventricular ectopics are the commonest. Atrial tachycardia with block is the signature: a fast atrium behind a blocked node. In a patient with atrial fibrillation the warning is a pulse that turns slow and regular, which means the node is completely blocked and a junctional focus has taken over. And bidirectional VT, where the axis of the wide beats alternates from one beat to the next. That was a grand test stem, with nausea, confusion and renal impairment: cardiac glycoside toxicity. What digoxin does not cause is atrial fibrillation racing through the node, because the node is the thing it blocks.

Now potassium, which has two faces. In an acute overdose pumps are blocked all over the body, potassium cannot enter cells, and the serum level rises. So the potassium measures how much pump is poisoned. A level above five predicts death better than the bradycardia, the block or the digoxin level, and it is an indication for the antidote. That was the question you missed: you chose bradycardia.

In chronic toxicity it is the reverse. The elderly patient on a diuretic has a low potassium, and digoxin and potassium compete for the same site on the pump, so with less potassium more digoxin binds. A low magnesium and a high calcium do the same harm.

[[Acute digoxin overdose: a potassium above five marks severity and calls for Fab. Chronic toxicity: a low potassium, a low magnesium or a high calcium brings it on.]]

The antidote is digoxin-specific Fab, the binding fragment of an antibody, which pulls the drug off the pump. Every source agrees on three indications: a life-threatening arrhythmia, a cardiac arrest, and a potassium above five. Many add organ hypoperfusion, a very high level, and a large ingestion: over ten milligrams in an adult or four in a child. Fab also brings the potassium down, so it replaces calcium as the treatment of that hyperkalaemia.

And the second miss. A digoxin arrest in pulseless electrical activity, with Fab given during prolonged resuscitation. You chose that Fab is ineffective during arrest. The key was that return of circulation may follow even delayed Fab. Give it and keep compressing.

One mimic. Bidirectional VT in a young person on no digoxin, fainting on exertion, is catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, an inherited calcium leak, where beta-blockers come first.

Digoxin was slow and fast together. The next two drug families are simply slow.
lesson.cap: Digoxin effect: scooped ST, short QT (not toxicity). Toxicity: ectopy plus block; bidirectional VT is the signature.

steps.bridge: Class two and class four in excess. Next, the poisons with no class of their own.

lesson.text:
Beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers are class two and class four given in excess, and they meet at the same place: the calcium cell of the node and the calcium channel of the muscle.

Recall the chain. The beta receptor raises cyclic AMP, which opens more L-type calcium channels and steepens phase four. A beta-blocker cuts the signal at the top. A calcium-channel blocker shuts the channel at the bottom. Either way the node fires slowly, the AV node conducts slowly and the muscle contracts weakly. So the shared ECG is a sinus bradycardia, a long PR, then higher grades of AV block and junctional rhythms, with a narrow QRS.

Now the differences, and each one is a question.

Among the beta-blockers two are special. Propranolol also blocks sodium channels, so it widens the QRS and causes seizures, and that part answers to bicarbonate. Sotalol also blocks potassium channels, so it lengthens the QT and causes torsades. Those are the two beta-blockers with an extra class hidden inside them.

Among the calcium-channel blockers the split is by tissue. Verapamil acts most on the heart: it is the strongest depressant of the node and the muscle. The dihydropyridines, nifedipine and amlodipine, act most on the vessels. Diltiazem sits between them on both. A grand test asked which drug has minimal cardiac depression with intermediate vasodilation. The key was diltiazem, and you chose nimodipine. Nimodipine and nifedipine do depress the heart least of all, but they are the strongest vasodilators, not intermediate ones. The word intermediate is what picks diltiazem: less depressant than verapamil, and less dilating than a dihydropyridine.

{{**Drug | Heart | Vessels**
Verapamil | strongest | moderate
Diltiazem | less | intermediate
Amlodipine, nifedipine | least | strongest}}

So a verapamil or diltiazem overdose is slow, blocked and failing. An amlodipine overdose is a different picture: dilated vessels, warm skin, a low pressure, a pump that still works and a reflex sinus tachycardia. That is vasoplegia, and the question from the shock packets applies: is the fault the pump or the squeeze? Here it is the squeeze, so the first vasoactive drug is noradrenaline. On that grand test question you chose phenylephrine alone.

[[Verapamil and diltiazem poison the pump and the node: slow, blocked, weak. Amlodipine poisons the vessels: warm, vasodilated, fast, and the first drug is noradrenaline.]]

One blood test separates the two families. The beta cell of the pancreas releases insulin through the same L-type calcium channel. Block it and insulin falls, so a calcium-channel-blocker overdose has a high glucose, in an alert patient. A beta-blocker overdose has a low or normal glucose, in a drowsy one.

That same fact explains the treatment you missed. A stressed heart switches its fuel from fatty acids to glucose, and it needs insulin to take glucose in. The poisoned patient has too little insulin. High-dose insulin gives the heart its fuel back, and contraction improves without extra oxygen demand.

[[High-dose insulin works in calcium-channel-blocker shock by restoring the heart's use of glucose. It does not open calcium channels. And calcium, glucagon and insulin all leave a wide QRS untouched.]]

Three short ones to finish. Glucagon reaches cyclic AMP through its own receptor, past the blocked beta receptor. Levosimendan works from further down: it makes the contractile proteins more sensitive to calcium and opens potassium channels in the vessels, with no receptor involved, so it still works in a patient on beta-blockers. That was a grand test miss, and you met the drug in the second shock packet. And sustained-release verapamil, taken three hours ago by a patient who still looks well, keeps absorbing for a day: the keyed decontamination is whole-bowel irrigation, not a single dose of charcoal.

The doses and the order are in the cardiac drugs packet. Next, the poisons that have no class of their own.

steps.bridge: Every poison was a channel or a nerve. Last: cold, heat and hormones on the same trace.

lesson.text:
There is no new mechanism in this card. Each of these poisons presses on something you have already met, so for each one name the channel or the nerve before the ECG.

Organophosphates first, because of your missed question. They block the enzyme that clears acetylcholine, so acetylcholine floods every synapse. The ECG goes through three phases. Early, the nicotinic receptors of the sympathetic ganglia fire, so there is a brief sinus tachycardia and hypertension. Then the muscarinic effect, the vagus written large, takes over: sinus bradycardia, a long PR, AV block. And then, over the following days, the QT lengthens with ST and T changes, and polymorphic VT or torsades can appear, sometimes when the patient seems to be improving. A long QTc is common, and it travels with respiratory failure and death. So a QTc of four hundred and seventy may indicate increased severity. It does not confirm it, and it does not predict atropine resistance.

[[Organophosphate ECG in three phases: a brief tachycardia, then vagal bradycardia and block, then a long QT with torsades days later. A long QTc may indicate greater severity; it does not prove it.]]

Lithium. Its commonest change is harmless: flat or inverted T waves, like those of a low potassium, because lithium takes potassium's place inside the cell. In toxicity it suppresses the sinus node: sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial block, pauses. It can lengthen the QT and unmask a Brugada pattern. And one fact from a grand test you missed: seizures in severe lithium toxicity are treated first with a benzodiazepine, not phenytoin.

Antipsychotics. A long QT from hERG block, a sinus tachycardia from their anticholinergic action, and with thioridazine a wide QRS as well.

Theophylline and caffeine. They block adenosine receptors and raise cyclic AMP, a beta stimulus without the receptor. So: sinus tachycardia, multifocal atrial tachycardia, supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, with a low potassium from the shift into cells. Adenosine will not work, because its receptor is occupied. For the fast supraventricular rhythms a short-acting beta-blocker such as esmolol is the textbook choice. For ventricular irritability with haemodynamic compromise your grand test keyed amiodarone, and you got it right. Cimetidine is the wrong option: it raises the theophylline level.

Cocaine is three poisons in one: a sympathetic storm with coronary spasm and infarction, a sodium-channel blocker with a wide QRS, and a long QT.

Then the short list. Arsenic trioxide: a long QT and torsades. Carbon monoxide: ischaemic ST and T changes, because the heart is starved of oxygen. Hydrofluoric acid: fluoride binds calcium and magnesium and the potassium rises, so a long QT and then ventricular fibrillation. High-dose loperamide and the sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine: both a wide QRS and a long QT.

{{**Poison | ECG**
Organophosphate | brady, AV block, later long QT
Lithium | flat T, sinus node pauses
Theophylline | tachycardias, MAT, low K⁺
Arsenic, hydrofluoric acid | long QT
Loperamide, diphenhydramine | wide QRS and long QT}}

So every poison was a channel or a nerve you knew. One last card: what cold, heat and hormones do to the same trace.

Cold slows every channel in the heart, so hypothermia is the one condition that lengthens every interval at once. That is the anchor for this last card.

Follow the heart as it cools. First comes shivering, seen as a fine tremor of the baseline. Then the sinus node, the first tissue to be depressed, slows: sinus bradycardia. Then atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular rate. All the while the PR, the QRS and the QT lengthen together.

And then the wave that names the condition. At the J point, where the QRS ends and the ST begins, a hump appears, pointing the same way as the QRS: the Osborn wave, or J wave. Where does it come from? From phase one again, the notch made by the brief outward potassium current, deepest in the epicardium. Cold slows the calcium current that normally cancels the notch, so in the epicardium the notch deepens while the endocardium is unchanged. That difference across the wall, at the very end of the QRS, is the J wave. It is the same notch that, exaggerated in the right ventricular outflow tract, draws Brugada. You see it best in the inferior leads and the chest leads from V3 to V6, and it is upside down in aVR. Its height grows as the temperature falls.

[[Hypothermia: sinus bradycardia, then slow atrial fibrillation, long PR, QRS and QT, and the Osborn wave at the J point, taller as the patient gets colder. Below twenty-eight degrees the danger is ventricular fibrillation.]]

The numbers are rough. Osborn waves and atrial fibrillation appear below about thirty-two degrees. Below twenty-eight the ventricle is irritable and rough handling can tip it into fibrillation. Below about twenty-four comes standstill. The arrest packet gives you the grades and the rewarming.

{{**Core temperature | ECG**
Below 35 °C | shivering artefact, sinus bradycardia
Below 32 °C | slow AF, Osborn wave, long PR, QRS, QT
Below 28 °C | VF risk
Below about 24 °C | asystole}}

Two reminders. A J wave at a normal temperature is hypercalcaemia, or early repolarisation. And the cold ECG can hide a high potassium.

Now heat and hormones, each in a line, because each is a loop back.

Fever and thyroid storm are sympathetic drive: sinus tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation in between one in ten and one in four hyperthyroid patients, more in the elderly. Myxoedema is the cold heart without the cold: sinus bradycardia, low voltage, flat T waves, a long QT, sometimes AV block, and a pericardial effusion, which you met with low voltage in the first packet. Adrenal crisis shows through its potassium: with no aldosterone, the peaked T waves of hyperkalaemia, on low voltage. Phaeochromocytoma is catecholamine excess: sinus tachycardia, arrhythmias, and after a surge the deep T inversion and long QT of a stunned ventricle. And a rising intracranial pressure gives the Cushing response, a slow pulse with a high pressure.

Step back, because this ends the two ECG packets. Nothing you heard changed the trace in a new way. Every ion, drug, poison and hormone worked through a phase of the action potential, through the two kinds of cell, or through the position of a camera.

[[Everything that changes the ECG acts on a phase of the action potential, on the node or the wiring below it, or on what a lead can see. QRS is sodium, ST is calcium, T is potassium, QT is the whole cell.]]

You can now read the wiring, the waves and the cameras. Next comes the one event where all three are tested together: a coronary artery closes, and the infarct writes itself on the ECG.
lesson.cap: Hypothermia: Osborn (J) wave at the end of the QRS grows as the temperature falls; bradycardia and long PR, QRS and QT.

spine: An overdose is an antiarrhythmic class in excess: wide QRS = sodium, long QT = potassium (hERG), slow with long PR = the nodes.
Na⁺-channel poison: QRS ≥100 ms (seizures), ≥160 ms (VT), terminal R in aVR ≥3 mm → NaHCO₃ 1–2 mmol/kg; never class Ia/Ic, physostigmine, phenytoin.
Digoxin: effect = scooped ST, short QT. Toxicity = ectopy plus block, bidirectional VT. Acute K⁺ >5 → Fab; chronic: low K⁺ worsens it.
β-blocker and verapamil/diltiazem: bradycardia, AV block, weak pump (insulin restores glucose use). Amlodipine: vasoplegia → noradrenaline.
OP: tachycardia → bradycardia and block → long QT. Lithium: flat T, sinus pauses. Theophylline: tachyarrhythmias, adenosine fails.
Hypothermia: bradycardia → slow AF → Osborn wave, all intervals long → VF below 28 °C. Every change maps to a phase or a camera.

close.text:
So let's walk back through it, from the slow heart to the poisoned one.

The blocks came first, and one sentence carried them all. The level decides everything. In the calcium node, conduction tires gradually: the PR stretches, a beat drops, and atropine helps. Below the node, in the sodium wiring, conduction fails all at once: the PR stays fixed, the QRS is often wide, and atropine is no help. Pace. Complete block was the two clocks running apart, and the width of the escape told you where the break lay. The bundle branches were the same idea one level lower, and the left bundle hid the infarct until Sgarbossa found it.

Then the short circuits. A loop through the node breaks at the node, with a vagal manoeuvre or adenosine. A loop that doesn't use the node, like flutter, is only unmasked. And a pathway that bypasses the node turns every nodal blocker into a danger.

Then the drugs, each one a phase. [[Class one touches sodium and widens the QRS. Class two and class four slow the node and lengthen the PR. Class three blocks potassium and lengthens the QT.]]

And last, what changes the waves from outside. Potassium peaks the T and then widens everything. Calcium moves the ST. The QT is the whole cell, and anything that blocks potassium leaving can stretch it into torsades. Sodium-channel poisons widen the QRS and swing its tail towards aVR. Digoxin speeds the ectopy and slows the node at the same time.

Now the traps.

One. Wolff–Parkinson–White with a regular, narrow tachycardia. The tempting answer is that nodal drugs are banned. The node is part of this circuit. Vagal manoeuvre, adenosine, then a nodal blocker. You missed this one. The ban is for pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

Two. Unstable Mobitz two. The tempting first drug is atropine. The block lies below the node, where the vagus doesn't reach. Pace through the skin as the bridge.

Three. Congenital long QT, going for an anaesthetic. The tempting answer is sevoflurane. Volatile agents lengthen the QT. Propofol is the safe agent. You missed this one too.

Four. A tricyclic overdose in a child. The tempting answer is a different cut-off for children. It's the same one hundred milliseconds, and a child's QRS is normally narrower, so one hundred is clearly wide.

Five. Acute digoxin overdose. The tempting marker of severity is the bradycardia or the level. [[In acute digoxin poisoning, a potassium above five is the marker of severity and an indication for Fab.]] And Fab still works in an arrest, so give it and keep compressing.

And six. Torsades. The tempting drug is amiodarone. It blocks potassium and lengthens the QT further. Give magnesium, raise the rate, and stop the drug that caused it.

The check comes up on the next screen. Answer each in your head before you tap it open.

You can now read the wiring, the waves and the cameras. The next packet puts all three to work on one patient. The infarct, where an artery closes, a wall is injured, and the ECG has to tell you before the troponin can.

drill.q: In Wenckebach, what happens to the R-R interval before the dropped beat, and which PR is longest?
drill.a: The R-R **shortens** (the PR increment shrinks). The longest PR is just before the drop, the shortest just after; the pause is less than two P-P.

drill.q: Atropine, exercise and carotid massage: effect on a nodal vs an infranodal block?
drill.a: Atropine and exercise **improve nodal** and **worsen infranodal** block. Carotid massage does the opposite.

drill.q: 2:1 AV block in a sleeping athlete with a narrow QRS: level?
drill.a: **AV node.** 2:1 block cannot be classified by PR; narrow QRS + vagal setting = nodal. Wide QRS or anterior MI = His–Purkinje.

drill.q: Complete heart block: narrow escape at 50 vs wide escape at 30?
drill.a: Narrow, 40–60 = junctional, block in the node (inferior MI), some atropine response. Wide, 20–40 = ventricular, infranodal (anterior MI), unreliable: pace.

drill.q: Which infarct causes more AV block, and which block is worse?
drill.a: **Inferior MI** causes more block of every degree (nodal, transient). **Anterior MI** block is rarer but infranodal and needs pacing.

drill.q: Unstable Mobitz II: first intervention? And the child with HR 46 and poor perfusion despite oxygenation?
drill.a: **Transcutaneous pacing** (bridge to transvenous). Child: **CPR + adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg**; atropine only for vagal tone or primary AV block.

drill.q: V1 shows rSR′ and the axis is −60°. Name it. What if RBBB and LBBB alternate?
drill.a: RBBB + left anterior fascicular block = **bifascicular block**. Alternating BBB = **permanent pacemaker, class I**, even without symptoms.

drill.q: Sgarbossa: the three criteria, points and cut-off?
drill.a: Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm (**5**); concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3 (**3**); discordant ST elevation ≥5 mm (**2**). **≥3** = MI. Smith: ST/S ≤ −0.25.

drill.q: Regular narrow tachycardia at 180 with inverted P at the tail of the QRS in II, III, aVF: mechanism?
drill.a: **AVNRT**, re-entry within the AV node (RP < 70 ms). AVRT has a separate P in the ST segment (RP > 70 ms).

drill.q: WPW with a regular narrow tachycardia vs WPW with an irregular wide tachycardia at 250: treatment?
drill.a: Orthodromic AVRT: **vagal → adenosine → nodal blocker**. Pre-excited AF: **procainamide/ibutilide or cardioversion; no nodal blockers, no IV amiodarone**.

drill.q: Regular narrow tachycardia at exactly 150; adenosine slows it and sawtooth waves appear. Diagnosis?
drill.a: **Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction** (atrial rate ~300). Adenosine unmasks, never cures.

drill.q: Severe aortic stenosis, new fast AF, pulmonary oedema within hours: mechanism? And the JVP in AF?
drill.a: **Loss of atrial systole** (atrial kick) in a stiff ventricle. AF has **no a wave**; complete heart block has cannon a waves.

drill.q: High potassium: what changes first on the ECG, and what changes next?
drill.a: First a tall, narrow, tented T with a short QT (faster phase 3). Then sodium channels inactivate: P flattens and vanishes, PR and QRS widen, sine wave.

drill.q: Normal anion gap acidosis with a potassium of 6.1 in a diabetic. Diagnosis?
drill.a: Type 4 RTA (hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism). Types 1 and 2 have a low potassium.

drill.q: ESRD, potassium 7.2, peaked T and widening QRS, emergency dialysis. Dialysate potassium?
drill.a: 1 mEq/L. Not zero.

drill.q: Calcium and the QT: which part of the QT changes?
drill.a: The ST segment only. Low calcium: long ST, long QT, normal T. High calcium: short ST, short QT.

drill.q: Potassium 2.4, magnesium low, ventricular ectopics, central line. Plan?
drill.a: Potassium in saline (not dextrose) at about 20 mEq/h with monitoring, plus magnesium at the same time.

drill.q: Bazett's formula and its fault?
drill.a: QTc = QT ÷ √RR in seconds. Overcorrects at fast rates, undercorrects at slow rates.

drill.q: Schwartz score: swimmer with syncope, QTc 485, relative with LQTS and another with sudden death under 30?
drill.a: 3 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 6.5: high probability (≥3.5). Without the relative with LQTS it is 5.5.

drill.q: Safe induction and maintenance agent in congenital long QT?
drill.a: Propofol. Volatiles including sevoflurane prolong the QTc; avoid ondansetron, droperidol and ketamine.

drill.q: Brugada type 1 ECG, and the treatment after a survived arrest?
drill.a: Coved ST elevation ≥2 mm with a negative T in V1–V2. ICD (class I); quinidine is the adjunct.

drill.q: Tricyclic overdose: the two QRS numbers, and the threshold in a child?
drill.a: ≥100 ms predicts seizures, ≥160 ms ventricular arrhythmia. The child's threshold for bicarbonate is the same, 100 ms.

drill.q: Wide-QRS tachycardia after cocaine, or propranolol with QRS 160 ms. Treatment?
drill.a: IV sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg. Not verapamil, a beta-blocker or glucagon.

drill.q: Acute digoxin overdose, potassium 5.8, bradycardia, normal pressure. What mandates Fab?
drill.a: The potassium above 5 mEq/L.

drill.q: Amlodipine overdose: warm, hypotensive, good contractility. First vasoactive drug? And why does high-dose insulin work in verapamil shock?
drill.a: Noradrenaline. Insulin restores myocardial glucose use; it does not open calcium channels.

drill.q: Three findings that prove a wide regular tachycardia is VT?
drill.a: **AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats.** If in doubt treat as VT; never verapamil.

drill.q: Vaughan Williams: which class widens the QRS, which lengthens the QT, which lengthen the PR? Sotalol's serious adverse effect?
