drill.a: Class I (Ic most) widens QRS; class III (and Ia) lengthens QT; classes II and IV lengthen PR. Sotalol: **QT prolongation and torsades**. Congenital LQTS anaesthetic: **propofol**.

drill.q: Organophosphate poisoning with QTc 470 ms: meaning?
drill.a: It may indicate increased severity. It does not confirm it or predict atropine resistance.

drill.q: Digoxin PEA arrest after prolonged CPR: is Fab still worth giving?
drill.a: Yes. ROSC may follow even delayed Fab; give it and keep compressing (GT8 Q54).

drill.q: Low-output shock in a patient on a chronic beta-blocker: which inotrope works past the receptor?
drill.a: Levosimendan (calcium sensitiser, K-ATP opener) or milrinone (PDE3); beta-agonists are blunted (GT8 Q82).

drill.q: Calcium-channel blocker with the least cardiac depression and intermediate vasodilation?
drill.a: Diltiazem. Verapamil is strongest on the heart; dihydropyridines strongest on the vessels (GT8 Q90).

drill.q: Sort into narrow/wide × regular/irregular: AVNRT, flutter with variable block, antidromic AVRT, polymorphic VT.
drill.a: Narrow regular; narrow irregular; wide regular; wide irregular (INI GT2 Q75).

drill.q: Severe lithium toxicity with seizures: first drug? And its usual ECG change?
drill.a: Benzodiazepines (GT8 Q73). T-wave flattening or inversion; also sinus node dysfunction and bradycardia.

traps.trap: In Wenckebach the R-R interval lengthens before the dropped beat
traps.truth: The PR lengthens but by a smaller increment each beat, so the R-R shortens; the pause is less than two P-P intervals and the PR after it is the shortest.

traps.trap: Atropine improves Mobitz II; carotid massage worsens it
traps.truth: Atropine and exercise improve nodal (Mobitz I) block and worsen or do not change infranodal (Mobitz II) block; carotid massage worsens nodal block and may improve infranodal block.

traps.trap: Constant P-P with a pause equal to two P-P intervals is a sinus arrest
traps.truth: An exact multiple means SA exit block type II; a sinus pause has no fixed relation to the P-P interval.

traps.trap: Sleeping athlete with 2:1 block: His bundle or bundle branch
traps.truth: 2:1 block cannot be typed by PR; narrow QRS in a vagal setting = AV node.

traps.trap: Asymptomatic first-degree AV block: admit or observe
traps.truth: PR > 0.20 s with every P conducted needs no treatment: discharge.

traps.trap: Anterior MI with second-degree block: Mobitz I, benign, give atropine
traps.truth: Wrong key (it contradicts its own explanation). LAD supplies the His–Purkinje system: infranodal block, wide escape, no atropine response, pacing (pads on, transvenous wire). Even if the strip shows PR lengthening, block in an anterior MI with a wide QRS is not 'benign, give atropine'.

traps.trap: Anterior MI most commonly produces second- and third-degree block
traps.truth: Inferior MI causes more AV block of every degree; anterior block is rarer but far more dangerous. Keyed true statement: transient AV block in 10–25% of MIs.

traps.trap: AV dissociation always means complete heart block
traps.truth: Only if the atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate. VT or an accelerated junctional rhythm faster than sinus gives dissociation without block.

traps.trap: Cannon a waves are a sign of atrial fibrillation
traps.truth: AF has no a wave at all (no atrial contraction). Intermittent cannon a waves and a variable S1 belong to complete heart block.

traps.trap: Unstable Mobitz II: atropine, or a transvenous pacemaker as the initial step
traps.truth: Transcutaneous pacing at once as the bridge to a transvenous wire; atropine acts on the node, not below it.

traps.trap: Child with HR 46 and poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation: atropine or dopamine
traps.truth: Start CPR and give adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg. Atropine is specifically indicated only for raised vagal tone or primary AV block.
traps.asked: Mini test, 22%; GT8 Q80 (complete AV block in a child: atropine)

traps.trap: Atropine for bradycardia in a transplanted heart; more atropine after 3 mg
traps.truth: The denervated heart has no vagal tone to block: isoprenaline, adrenaline or pacing. 3 mg is full vagal blockade; next is dopamine/adrenaline or pacing.

traps.trap: Adrenaline 2–10 µg/kg/min for bradycardia
traps.truth: 2–10 µg/min, not per kg. Dopamine is the per-kg one: 5–20 µg/kg/min.

traps.trap: Bradycardia on metoprolol and digoxin: the β-blocker alone explains it
traps.truth: Both act on the AV node and add up; digoxin is the synergistic culprit.

traps.trap: ST elevation in V1–V3 with LBBB (or a paced rhythm) is an anterior STEMI
traps.truth: Discordant ST elevation is expected in LBBB. Infarction is diagnosed by concordance (Sgarbossa ≥3) or excessive discordance (ST/S ≤ −0.25).

traps.trap: A Sgarbossa score of 0 excludes MI
traps.truth: Specificity >90% but sensitivity only about 20–35%: serial ECG, troponin and echo.

traps.trap: New LBBB with chest pain and shock: repeat the ECG or trend troponin
traps.truth: Instability is the first branch: treat as a STEMI equivalent (reperfusion). ESC 2023: BBB or paced rhythm with suspected ongoing ischaemia is managed like STEMI.

traps.trap: Alternating bundle branch block without symptoms can be observed
traps.truth: It proves disease in all three fascicles: permanent pacemaker, class I, with or without symptoms (ESC 2021). Bifascicular block + syncope: EP study, HV ≥70 ms = pacemaker.

traps.trap: Inverted P in II, III, aVF at 180/min: re-entry via an accessory pathway
traps.truth: Typical AVNRT: re-entry within the node, P buried in or at the tail of the QRS (RP < 70 ms). AVRT shows a separate P in the ST segment.

traps.trap: Asthmatic with SVT: adenosine
traps.truth: IV verapamil or diltiazem; adenosine can cause severe bronchospasm. And in any stable SVT the vagal manoeuvre comes before adenosine.

traps.trap: WPW with a regular narrow tachycardia: nodal blockers and adenosine are contraindicated
traps.truth: Orthodromic AVRT has the node in the loop: vagal manoeuvre, adenosine, then an AV-nodal blocker. The ban applies to pre-excited AF (irregular, wide).

traps.trap: Pre-excited AF: only verapamil is contraindicated; IV amiodarone is safe
traps.truth: Every nodal blocker is harmful (adenosine, β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) and so is IV amiodarone (ESC 2019 SVT class III; AHA 2025 class 3: harm for digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers and IV amiodarone). Give procainamide or ibutilide, or cardiovert. Mark verapamil if only one answer is allowed.
traps.asked: DocT GT AIM1 Q36 / GT4 Q56, 45–54%

traps.trap: Delta wave and short PR: dual AV nodal pathway
traps.truth: An accessory AV pathway. Dual nodal pathways cause AVNRT with a normal resting ECG.

traps.trap: Vagal manoeuvres: deep breath before straining; bilateral carotid massage; massage despite a bruit
traps.truth: Modified Valsalva is a sustained strain (40 mmHg, 15 s) then supine with legs raised (REVERT 43% vs 17%). Carotid massage: one side, 5–10 s, monitored, never with a bruit or prior TIA/stroke.

traps.trap: Adenosine via a central line: still 6 mg; adenosine is safe in any wide tachycardia
traps.truth: 3 mg (exam key; AHA 2025 says 1 mg may suffice) via central line, after transplant, with dipyridamole or carbamazepine. Only for regular monomorphic wide tachycardia, never irregular or polymorphic.

traps.trap: Regular narrow tachycardia at 150 is sinus tachycardia; adenosine cures flutter
traps.truth: 150 regular = flutter with 2:1 conduction until proven otherwise; adenosine only unmasks the sawtooth waves at 300.

traps.trap: Severe aortic stenosis with new AF and pulmonary oedema: acute coronary thrombosis
traps.truth: Loss of atrial systole (atrial kick) in a stiff, preload-dependent ventricle, with a shortened filling time.

traps.trap: AF that has become slow and regular on digoxin is good rate control
traps.truth: Regularised AF = complete heart block with a junctional escape: digoxin toxicity.

traps.trap: AVRT or AVNRT listed as a cause of an irregular tachycardia; pre-excited AF filed as regular
traps.truth: Node-dependent loops are always regular. Narrow irregular = AF, flutter with variable block, MAT. Wide irregular = pre-excited AF, AF with BBB, polymorphic VT.

traps.trap: Wide QRS, no P waves, rate 150 in ischaemic heart disease: flutter, AF or SVT; give verapamil
traps.truth: Regular and wide with prior MI is VT until proven otherwise. If in doubt treat as VT; verapamil can cause collapse.

traps.trap: Fine VF is too late to shock
traps.truth: Fine VF is still shockable; check gain and leads before calling asystole.

traps.trap: Sotalol's main adverse effect is bradycardia or hypotension
traps.truth: QT prolongation and torsades, from potassium-channel (class III) block.

traps.trap: Sevoflurane (or any agent) is safe in congenital long QT; ondansetron for nausea
traps.truth: Propofol is the safe agent. Volatiles including sevoflurane, ondansetron and droperidol prolong QTc.

traps.trap: Flecainide to suppress ectopics after MI or in structural heart disease
traps.truth: Class Ic is proarrhythmic in scarred ventricles (CAST: excess deaths). Structurally normal hearts only, with a nodal blocker in AF/flutter.

traps.trap: Peaked T waves are a sign of digoxin toxicity
traps.truth: Peaked T = hyperkalaemia. Digoxin gives a scooped ST and short QT; toxicity gives ectopy plus block.

traps.trap: A normal ECG means a high potassium is safe, and the level predicts the ECG stage
traps.truth: The ECG is an unreliable guide to the level and stages can be skipped; any ECG change means calcium first. The trace sets urgency, not the number.

traps.trap: Calcium gluconate lowers the serum potassium
traps.truth: It only restores the gap between resting and threshold potential for 30–60 min; potassium is unchanged until it is shifted or removed.

traps.trap: Normal anion gap acidosis with hyperkalaemia = type 1 or type 2 RTA
traps.truth: NAGMA with a high potassium is type 4 RTA (low aldosterone effect); types 1 and 2 are hypokalaemic.

traps.trap: Zero-potassium dialysate for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
traps.truth: Keyed answer 1 mEq/L: a low bath but not zero, because too rapid a fall in potassium is arrhythmogenic.

traps.trap: Suxamethonium is safe in a burn or spinal injury once the patient is stable
traps.truth: From 24–48 h after burns, denervation or prolonged immobility, extrajunctional receptors let potassium rise by 5–10 mmol/L; the normal rise is 0.5.

traps.trap: Withhold IV calcium in symptomatic hypocalcaemia because the patient is on digoxin
traps.truth: Give IV calcium gluconate slowly with ECG monitoring and correct magnesium.

traps.trap: The QT is long in hypercalcaemia
traps.truth: High calcium shortens the ST and the QT; low calcium lengthens the ST with a normal T. Very high calcium can add J (Osborn) waves at normal temperature.

traps.trap: Severe hypercalcaemia with renal failure and low EF: aggressive saline
traps.truth: No kidney to excrete it and no heart to tolerate it: haemodialysis.

traps.trap: Hypokalaemia with hypomagnesaemia and ectopy: potassium in dextrose, or potassium at 50 mEq/h, or defer potassium until magnesium is normal
traps.truth: Potassium in saline at about 20 mEq/h by central line with monitoring, together with magnesium: low magnesium keeps the renal potassium channel (ROMK) open.

traps.trap: Bazett's formula is accurate at all heart rates
traps.truth: It overcorrects at fast rates and undercorrects at slow rates; Fridericia is better at the extremes.

traps.trap: Schwartz score: adding syncope and torsades together, or both family items from one relative
traps.truth: QTc ≥480 = 3, syncope with stress = 2, torsades = 2; ≥3.5 is high probability. Swimmer with syncope, QTc 485 and family history was keyed 6.5 (3 + 2 + 1 + 0.5), which needs two relatives: one with definite LQTS (1) and another with sudden death under 30 (0.5). With a family sudden death alone the strict sum is 5.5; pick 5.5 if offered, 6.5 if not.

traps.trap: Sevoflurane (or any agent) is fine for general anaesthesia in congenital long QT
traps.truth: Propofol is the keyed safe agent; volatiles prolong QTc; avoid ondansetron, droperidol, ketamine; continue the beta-blocker.

traps.trap: QTc prolongation in organophosphate poisoning confirms severe poisoning or predicts atropine resistance
traps.truth: It may indicate increased severity (associated with respiratory failure and mortality) but does not confirm it.

traps.trap: Amiodarone (or sotalol, procainamide) for torsades; synchronised cardioversion for polymorphic VT
traps.truth: Torsades: magnesium 2 g, faster rate, stop QT drugs. Sustained polymorphic VT: unsynchronised shock. Amiodarone only when the QT is normal (ischaemia).

traps.trap: Brugada has a positive T wave in the right precordial leads; quinidine gives the greatest reduction in sudden death
traps.truth: Type 1 is coved ST ≥2 mm with a negative T in V1–V2. After a survived arrest the answer is an ICD (class I); quinidine is the adjunct.
traps.asked: GT7 Q130 (blank); Cardiac mini Oct Q2, Q7 (57%)

traps.trap: Children need a different (higher or lower) QRS cut-off for bicarbonate in tricyclic poisoning
traps.truth: The same 100 ms threshold applies; a child's normal QRS is narrower, so 100 ms is clearly wide.

traps.trap: Wide-QRS tachycardia after cocaine: verapamil or metoprolol
traps.truth: It is sodium-channel block: IV sodium bicarbonate, then lidocaine.

traps.trap: Propranolol overdose with a wide QRS: glucagon, insulin or calcium will narrow it
traps.truth: Propranolol is the membrane-stabilising beta-blocker; a QRS of 160 ms needs sodium bicarbonate.

traps.trap: Wide-complex tachycardia in tricyclic overdose: procainamide, flecainide, physostigmine or phenytoin
traps.truth: All worsen it. Bicarbonate first, lidocaine second line, benzodiazepine for seizures.

traps.trap: In acute digoxin overdose the bradycardia, AV block or digoxin level marks severity and mandates Fab
traps.truth: Potassium above 5 mEq/L is the prognostic marker and the indication for Fab.

traps.trap: Fab is useless once a digoxin-poisoned patient is in cardiac arrest
traps.truth: ROSC may follow even delayed Fab given during prolonged CPR: give it and continue CPR.

traps.trap: The scooped ST or a peaked T wave means digoxin toxicity
traps.truth: Scooped ST and short QT are digoxin effect. Peaked T is hyperkalaemia. Toxicity is ectopy plus block; bidirectional VT is cardiac glycoside toxicity.
traps.asked: GT7 Q100; Cardiac mini Oct Q11 (24%)

traps.trap: High-dose insulin works in calcium-channel-blocker poisoning by directly activating calcium channels
traps.truth: It restores myocardial glucose uptake and use: inotropy without extra oxygen demand.

traps.trap: Amlodipine overdose with warm vasodilated shock: dobutamine, phenylephrine alone or pacing
traps.truth: Dihydropyridine poisoning is vasoplegia with a preserved pump: noradrenaline first.

traps.trap: Nimodipine or nifedipine is the calcium-channel blocker with minimal cardiac depression and intermediate vasodilation
traps.truth: Diltiazem. Verapamil is strongest on the heart; dihydropyridines are weakest on the heart but strongest on vessels, so they are not 'intermediate'; diltiazem is in between on both.

traps.trap: Sustained-release verapamil overdose, patient well at 3 h: single-dose charcoal or lavage
traps.truth: Whole-bowel irrigation.

traps.trap: An inotrope cannot work in a patient on beta-blockers
traps.truth: Levosimendan acts beyond the receptor (calcium sensitiser, K-ATP opener), as do milrinone and glucagon.

traps.trap: Seizures in severe lithium toxicity: phenytoin
traps.truth: Benzodiazepines first.

traps.trap: Adenosine for a tachyarrhythmia in theophylline poisoning
traps.truth: Theophylline blocks adenosine receptors, so adenosine fails. Esmolol for SVT; the GT keyed amiodarone for ventricular irritability with compromise.

traps.trap: Reading the hypermagnesaemia ladder (4, 5, 10, 13) in mmol/L
traps.truth: Those figures are mEq/L (Marino): reflexes reduced >4, first-degree block >5, complete block >10, arrest >13 mEq/L; halve them for mmol/L.

mimics.pair: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II
mimics.tell: The PR before the dropped beat: lengthening in Mobitz I, constant in Mobitz II.

mimics.pair: Mobitz II vs blocked premature atrial beats
mimics.tell: In Mobitz II the non-conducted P is on time; a blocked PAC is early and deforms the preceding T wave.

mimics.pair: SA exit block type II vs sinus pause
mimics.tell: Exit block: the pause is an exact multiple of the P-P interval; a sinus pause is not.

mimics.pair: Sinus bradycardia vs junctional rhythm
mimics.tell: Upright P with a normal PR before each QRS vs inverted, absent or retrograde P with a narrow QRS.

mimics.pair: Complete heart block vs AV dissociation without block
mimics.tell: Which chamber is faster: atria faster = block; ventricles faster (VT, accelerated junctional) = no block.

mimics.pair: Nodal vs infranodal complete block (inferior vs anterior MI)
mimics.tell: The escape: narrow at 40–60 (junctional) vs wide at 20–40 (ventricular).

mimics.pair: RBBB vs LBBB
mimics.tell: The end of the QRS in V1: upright R′ in RBBB, downward (QS or deep S) in LBBB.

mimics.pair: LBBB vs RV-paced rhythm
mimics.tell: A pacing spike before each wide LBBB-shaped complex.

mimics.pair: Left anterior fascicular block vs old inferior MI
mimics.tell: Inferior leads begin with a small r (rS) in LAFB and with a Q in inferior MI.

mimics.pair: LBBB alone vs LBBB with MI
mimics.tell: Concordant ST change (same direction as the QRS), or discordant ST elevation ≥ 25% of the S wave.

mimics.pair: AVNRT vs orthodromic AVRT
mimics.tell: Where the retrograde P sits: hidden in or at the tail of the QRS (RP < 70 ms) vs separate in the ST segment (RP > 70 ms).

mimics.pair: Orthodromic AVRT vs pre-excited AF in WPW
mimics.tell: Regular and narrow (node in the loop: nodal blockers allowed) vs irregular and wide (nodal blockers banned).

mimics.pair: Pre-excited AF vs VT
mimics.tell: Pre-excited AF is irregular with QRS width changing beat to beat; VT is regular with uniform complexes.

mimics.pair: Flutter with 2:1 block vs AVNRT
mimics.tell: Adenosine: flutter slows and shows sawtooth waves, then resumes; AVNRT terminates.

mimics.pair: AF vs multifocal atrial tachycardia
mimics.tell: Both irregular; MAT has distinct P waves of three or more shapes, AF has none.

mimics.pair: Ashman beat vs ventricular ectopic in AF
mimics.tell: An aberrant (RBBB-shaped) beat ending a short cycle that follows a long one.

mimics.pair: VT vs SVT with aberrancy
mimics.tell: AV dissociation (with capture or fusion beats) proves VT.

mimics.pair: Fine VF vs asystole
mimics.tell: Fine VF shows low irregular waves at higher gain in two leads; asystole stays flat.

mimics.pair: Digoxin effect vs hyperkalaemia
mimics.tell: Scooped ST with a short QT vs a tall, narrow, peaked T wave.

mimics.pair: Peaked T of hyperkalaemia vs prominent U wave of hypokalaemia
mimics.tell: Hyperkalaemia: the tall narrow wave is the T itself, with a short QT. Hypokalaemia: the T is flat and the tall wave comes after it.

mimics.pair: Long QT of hypocalcaemia vs long QT of hypokalaemia or QT drugs
mimics.tell: Hypocalcaemia: long flat ST with a normal T. Hypokalaemia and hERG blockers: the T itself is flat or wide, with a U wave.

mimics.pair: Hyperkalaemia vs sodium-channel-blocker poisoning (both wide QRS)
mimics.tell: Hyperkalaemia: peaked T, absent P, slow rate. Sodium-channel blocker: sinus tachycardia with a tall terminal R in aVR.

mimics.pair: Sinoventricular rhythm of hyperkalaemia vs complete heart block with ventricular escape
mimics.tell: Both are slow and wide without conducted P waves; tented T waves and a high potassium mark hyperkalaemia, marching dissociated P waves mark complete block.

mimics.pair: Type 4 RTA vs types 1 and 2 RTA
mimics.tell: All are normal anion gap acidoses; only type 4 has a high potassium.

mimics.pair: LQT1 vs LQT2 vs LQT3
mimics.tell: The trigger: exercise or swimming (1), sudden noise or postpartum (2), sleep (3).

mimics.pair: Torsades vs ischaemic polymorphic VT
mimics.tell: The QT on the sinus beats: long = torsades (magnesium, never amiodarone); normal = ischaemia (revascularise, amiodarone or lidocaine).

mimics.pair: Brugada vs catecholaminergic polymorphic VT
mimics.tell: Brugada: abnormal resting ECG, death at rest, sleep or fever. CPVT: normal resting ECG, death on exertion, bidirectional VT.

mimics.pair: LQT3 vs Brugada (same gene, SCN5A)
mimics.tell: LQT3 is gain of function (late sodium leak, long QT). Brugada is loss of function (coved ST in V1–V2, normal QT).

mimics.pair: Wide QRS vs long QT in poisoning
mimics.tell: Wide QRS = sodium channel = bicarbonate. Long QT = potassium channel = magnesium and stop the drug.

mimics.pair: Digoxin effect vs digoxin toxicity
mimics.tell: Effect is a shape (scooped ST, short QT). Toxicity is a rhythm (ectopy plus block).

mimics.pair: Bidirectional VT: digoxin toxicity vs CPVT
mimics.tell: Digoxin: older patient on the drug, nausea, renal impairment, high potassium. CPVT: young, exertional syncope, no drug; beta-blockers first line.

mimics.pair: Calcium-channel-blocker vs beta-blocker overdose
mimics.tell: Glucose and mental state: CCB = hyperglycaemia in an alert patient; beta-blocker = low or normal glucose in a drowsy one.

mimics.pair: Verapamil or diltiazem overdose vs amlodipine overdose
mimics.tell: Heart rate and pump: verapamil = bradycardia, block, weak pump. Amlodipine = reflex tachycardia, warm vasoplegia, preserved pump.

mimics.pair: Osborn wave of hypothermia vs J wave of hypercalcaemia vs Brugada
mimics.tell: Temperature and leads: hypothermia is cold with bradycardia and long intervals, widespread; hypercalcaemia has a short QT at normal temperature; Brugada is confined to V1–V2 with a negative T.

new_cards.topic: The level decides: block in the node vs block below it
new_cards.q:
**For AV block at the node vs below the node, give:**
a The cell type at each level and how it fails
b The ECG pattern each produces
c The Wenckebach details (PR, R-R, pause)
d The effect of atropine, exercise and carotid massage on each
e Course and treatment
a: **AV node = calcium (slow) cells:** decremental conduction, so it tires gradually → **first degree and Mobitz I**. **His–Purkinje = sodium (fast) cells:** all-or-none conduction → **Mobitz II**.
**Mobitz I (Wenckebach):** PR lengthens beat by beat until one P is not conducted. **Mobitz II:** PR **constant** before and after a suddenly dropped beat (the P is on time).
**Wenckebach details:** longest PR just **before** the drop, shortest just **after**; **R-R shortens** before the pause (the PR increment shrinks); the pause is **< 2 × P-P**.
**QRS:** usually **narrow** in nodal block, often **wide** in infranodal block (bundle-branch disease). Mobitz II is always infranodal; Mobitz I with a wide QRS is occasionally infranodal.
**Atropine and exercise** speed the node: nodal block **improves**; infranodal block is **unchanged or worse** (faster atrial rate, same diseased wire).
**Carotid massage** does the opposite: nodal block **worsens**; infranodal block **may improve** (slower sinus rate gives His–Purkinje more recovery time).

**Nodal causes:** vagal tone (sleep, athletes), **inferior MI** (RCA), β-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, amiodarone → benign, observe, atropine if symptomatic. **Infranodal causes:** degenerative fibrosis, **anterior MI** (LAD) → progresses to complete block, **pace**.
new_cards.why: Foundation for every AV-block question; GT1 Q24 (AV block statements, missed); Marrow + DocT GT ask the atropine / carotid massage discriminator.

new_cards.topic: Complete heart block: two clocks, and the escape tells you the level
new_cards.q:
**For complete (third-degree) heart block, give:**
a The ECG definition
b How it differs from AV dissociation
c What the escape rhythm tells you
d The bedside signs
e Causes worth looking for
f Immediate treatment
a: **ECG:** regular P waves at the sinus rate, regular QRS at a slower independent rate, **no relationship** (PR varies at random); **atrial rate > ventricular rate**.

**AV dissociation is the wider term:** atria and ventricles beat independently. If the **ventricular rate is faster** (VT, accelerated junctional rhythm) it is dissociation by usurpation, **not block**.
**Junctional escape:** narrow QRS, **40–60/min**, fairly reliable, some response to atropine → block in the **AV node** (inferior MI, congenital with maternal anti-Ro).
**Ventricular escape:** wide QRS, **20–40/min**, unreliable, asystole risk → block in the **His–Purkinje** system (anterior MI, Lenègre–Lev fibrosis, post-TAVI).
**Bedside:** intermittent **cannon a waves** (atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve) and a **variable-intensity S1**. AF by contrast has **no a wave**.

**Causes:** degenerative fibrosis, MI, nodal drugs, hyperkalaemia, myocarditis, sarcoid, Lyme, hypothermia, post-cardiac surgery/TAVI; **new PR prolongation in aortic-valve endocarditis = root abscess**.
**Treatment:** transcutaneous pacing → transvenous wire; isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion as a bridge; atropine helps only a nodal (narrow-escape) block.
new_cards.why: Links the escape rhythm to the level of block; INI Sep-4 PYT Q44 (no a wave in AF vs cannon waves in complete block).

new_cards.topic: RBBB and LBBB built from the rule
new_cards.q:
**For right and left bundle branch block, give:**
a The QRS duration criteria
b RBBB: the pattern in V1 and V6, and why
c LBBB: the pattern in V1 and V6, and why
d The expected ST–T change in each
e What each means clinically
f Two look-alikes
a: **Complete block: QRS ≥ 0.12 s; incomplete: 0.10–0.12 s** with the same shape. The ventricle on the blocked side is activated late, muscle to muscle, so the **end of the QRS points to the blocked side**.
**RBBB:** septum and LV normal, RV late and rightward → **rSR′ ("M") in V1–V2**, **wide slurred S in I, aVL, V5–V6**; axis normal.
**LBBB:** septum now depolarises right to left (**no septal q in I, V5–V6**), LV late → **broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6**, **QS or rS in V1–V3**, poor R progression, often left axis.
**Secondary ST–T is discordant** (opposite to the terminal QRS): RBBB → T inversion V1–V3 is normal; LBBB → **ST elevation in V1–V3 is expected**, which hides infarction (use Sgarbossa).

**RBBB:** may be a normal variant; also RV strain, PE, ASD; **new RBBB in anterior MI = proximal LAD occlusion**. **LBBB:** almost always pathological (hypertension, IHD, cardiomyopathy, aortic stenosis, post-TAVI).
**RV apical pacing** = pacing spike + LBBB-like QRS. **Rate-related (aberrant) BBB** appears only at fast rates, usually RBBB shape because the right bundle recovers more slowly.
Mnemonic **WiLLiaM MaRRoW:** LBBB = W in V1, M in V6; RBBB = M in V1, W in V6.
new_cards.why: No card explained bundle branch block morphology; needed for Sgarbossa (MI-23/24), aberrancy vs VT and the paced ECG.

new_cards.topic: Fascicular blocks, bifascicular block and alternating bundle branch block
new_cards.q:
**For the fascicles of the left bundle, give:**
a Why the anterior fascicle is blocked more often
b The ECG of left anterior fascicular block
c The ECG of left posterior fascicular block
d Bifascicular and trifascicular block
e The two pacing rules (ESC 2021)
f LAFB vs inferior MI
a: **Three wires feed the ventricles:** right bundle, left anterior fascicle (long, thin, single LAD supply: **commonly blocked**), left posterior fascicle (short, broad, dual supply: **rarely blocked**).
**LAFB:** **left axis −45° or beyond**, qR in I and aVL, **rS in II, III, aVF**, QRS < 0.12 s; the commonest cause of left axis deviation. The axis swings towards the late-activated region.
**LPFB:** **right axis +90° or beyond**, rS in I and aVL, qR in II, III, aVF, QRS < 0.12 s; a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out RVH, lateral MI, PE).
**Bifascicular block** = RBBB + LAFB (commonest; both LAD-supplied) or RBBB + LPFB; LBBB also counts as two fascicles. RBBB with left axis = RBBB + LAFB.
**Trifascicular block** strictly = complete block or **alternating RBBB and LBBB**. Bifascicular block + long PR is loosely called trifascicular, but the PR delay may be in the AV node.
**Alternating bundle branch block → permanent pacemaker, class I, with or without symptoms.** **Bifascicular block + unexplained syncope → EP study; HV ≥ 70 ms → pacemaker** (normal HV 35–55 ms).
**LAFB vs old inferior MI:** both give left axis; LAFB inferior leads start with a small **r** (rS), inferior MI starts with a **Q** (QS or Qr).
new_cards.why: Fascicular and bifascicular block were mentioned by later cards (MI-60: new bifascicular block in anterior MI) with no card defining them; ESC 2021 pacing indications.

new_cards.topic: Three ways a rhythm goes wrong: automaticity, triggered activity and re-entry
new_cards.q:
**For the mechanisms of tachyarrhythmia, give:**
a Enhanced automaticity - mechanism and examples
b Triggered activity - the two afterdepolarisations
c Re-entry - the three requirements and four examples
d How each is broken
e The 2 × 2 grid (narrow/wide × regular/irregular)
a: **Automaticity:** steeper phase 4 (catecholamines, fever, hypoxia, ischaemia, hypokalaemia) → sinus tachycardia, focal atrial tachycardia, accelerated idioventricular rhythm after reperfusion (50–110/min, benign). Warms up and cools down; treat the cause.
**Early afterdepolarisation (phase 2–3):** needs a long action potential (long QT, bradycardia, low K⁺, low Mg²⁺) → **torsades de pointes**.
**Delayed afterdepolarisation (after phase 3):** intracellular calcium overload (digoxin, catecholamines, CPVT) → **bidirectional VT**.

**Re-entry** needs two pathways, **unidirectional block** in one, and **slow conduction** in the other so the first recovers. Starts and stops abruptly. **AVNRT** (within the node), **AVRT** (node + accessory pathway), **flutter** (cavotricuspid isthmus), **scar VT**.

**Breaking it:** node in the loop (AVNRT, AVRT) → vagal manoeuvre or adenosine **terminates**; node a bystander (flutter, atrial tachycardia) → adenosine only **unmasks**; any re-entry → cardioversion.
**Narrow regular:** sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT, atrial tachycardia, flutter with fixed block. **Narrow irregular:** AF, flutter with variable block, MAT.
**Wide regular:** VT, SVT with BBB/aberrancy, antidromic AVRT. **Wide irregular:** pre-excited AF, AF with BBB, polymorphic VT/torsades. **AVNRT and AVRT are never irregular.**
new_cards.why: INI GT2 Q75 (rhythm grid, missed; cohort 81%); the mechanism behind every tachycardia card in the Rhythm packet.

new_cards.topic: Flutter, AF and MAT on the ECG
new_cards.q:
**For the atrial tachyarrhythmias, give the ECG and the catch:**
a Typical atrial flutter
b Flutter with flecainide
c Atrial fibrillation
d What losing atrial contraction does
e Three patterns inside AF
f Multifocal atrial tachycardia
a: **Typical flutter:** macro re-entry round the tricuspid annulus (cavotricuspid isthmus), atrial rate **~300 (250–350)**; **sawtooth F waves**, negative in II, III, aVF, positive in V1, **no isoelectric baseline**.

**2:1 conduction → regular narrow tachycardia at ~150/min = flutter until proven otherwise.** Vagal manoeuvre or adenosine slows the ventricles and **reveals** the F waves; it never cures. Variable block makes flutter irregular.
**Class Ic drugs** slow the flutter rate (to ~200), letting the node conduct **1:1** with a wide QRS → always add an AV-nodal blocker.
**AF:** no P waves, fibrillatory baseline (atrial activity 350–600/min), **irregularly irregular** narrow QRS.
**No atrial contraction:** loss of atrial kick (severe aortic stenosis or any stiff LV + new fast AF → pulmonary oedema) and **no a wave** in the JVP/CVP trace.

**Ashman phenomenon:** aberrant (usually RBBB-shaped) beat ending a short cycle after a long one; not a PVC. **Very fast AF with wide, varying QRS = pre-excitation.** **Slow, regular AF on digoxin = complete block with junctional escape = toxicity.**
**MAT:** **≥ 3 P-wave morphologies**, varying PR, rate > 100, irregular; COPD, hypoxia, theophylline, low K⁺/Mg²⁺. Automaticity, so treat the cause; cardioversion does not help.
new_cards.why: GT8 Q16 (missed): severe AS + new AF → pulmonary oedema from loss of atrial systole; INI Sep-4 PYT Q44 (no a wave in AF); DocT GT flutter unmasked by adenosine.

new_cards.topic: Vaughan Williams as a map of the action potential
new_cards.q:
**For each Vaughan Williams class, give the current blocked, the ECG effect and the catch:**
a Class Ia, Ib, Ic
b Class II
c Class III
d Class IV
e The drugs outside the scheme
a: **Class I = sodium (phase 0) → QRS.** **Ia** (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide): intermediate kinetics + K⁺ block → **QRS and QT both lengthen**, torsades.
**Ib** (lidocaine, mexiletine): fast on-off, binds inactivated channels → works in **depolarised ischaemic ventricle**, little ECG change, useless in atrial arrhythmias.
**Ic** (flecainide, propafenone): slow off → **QRS widens most**, **use-dependent** (more block at fast rates); proarrhythmic with scar or structural disease (**CAST**: excess deaths post-MI).
**Class II = β-blockers:** flatter phase 4 and slower AV node → **slower rate, longer PR**; the class that reduces sudden death post-MI and in heart failure.

**Class III = potassium (phase 3) → QT longer.** Sotalol (also β-blocker; renal dosing), dofetilide, ibutilide: **reverse use-dependence** (torsades at slow rates). **Amiodarone** has class I–IV actions; torsades rare; thyroid, lung, liver toxicity. Dronedarone: harmful in severe HF.
**Class IV = verapamil, diltiazem:** nodal calcium upstroke → **slower rate, longer PR**, QRS and QT unchanged; negatively inotropic. Dihydropyridines are not antiarrhythmic.

**Outside:** adenosine (A1, IK-ACh: seconds of AV block); **digoxin** (Na-K ATPase block + vagal: long PR, scooped ST, short QT); magnesium (suppresses early afterdepolarisations: torsades); atropine; **ivabradine** (If: slows sinus node only; class 0 in the 2018 Oxford scheme).
new_cards.why: Naven named the antiarrhythmic classes as a foundation gap; NEET 2024 asked sotalol's adverse effect (QT prolongation); Marrow asks flecainide/CAST.

new_cards.topic: Choosing by substrate: which antiarrhythmic, and which never
new_cards.q:
**Which antiarrhythmic, and which never, for:**
a AF in a structurally normal heart
b Scarred or failing ventricle
c Pre-excited AF
d Torsades and congenital long QT (including the safe anaesthetic)
e Brugada syndrome
f A wide regular tachycardia of uncertain origin
a: **Structurally normal heart, AF rhythm control:** flecainide or propafenone **with an AV-nodal blocker** (prevents 1:1 flutter).
**Scar, IHD or HFrEF:** **amiodarone** (AF or VT; lidocaine as alternative in ischaemic VT). **Never** class Ic (CAST), verapamil/diltiazem (negative inotropy) or dronedarone in severe HF.
**Pre-excited AF:** procainamide or ibutilide, cardioversion if unstable. **Never** adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blocker, digoxin or IV amiodarone.
**Acquired torsades:** magnesium 2 g, stop the QT drug, correct K⁺, raise the rate (pacing or isoprenaline). **Never** amiodarone, sotalol or procainamide.

**Congenital long QT:** non-selective β-blocker (**nadolol or propranolol**); avoid QT-prolonging drugs and isoprenaline. **Anaesthesia: propofol is safe**; sevoflurane and other volatiles, ondansetron and droperidol prolong QTc; avoid ketamine, suxamethonium and neostigmine–anticholinergic reversal.
**Brugada:** sodium-channel blockers (flecainide, procainamide, ajmaline) unmask and worsen it; treat fever. **Quinidine** (blocks Ito) is the one drug used; ICD after arrest.
**Wide regular tachycardia, origin unclear: treat as VT. Verapamil can cause collapse.**
new_cards.why: GT1 Q147 (missed, cohort 67%): safe anaesthetic in congenital LQTS = propofol; collects every 'contraindicated drug' stem in one place.

new_cards.topic: Potassium and the membrane: why high potassium peaks the T first and then widens everything
new_cards.q:
**Potassium and the ECG, from the membrane:**
a What sets the resting potential
b High K⁺: the first effect and its wave
c High K⁺: the second effect and its waves
d Low K⁺
e Why the ECG is an unreliable guide to the level
f What IV calcium does
a: **Resting potential (about −90 mV) = the K⁺ gradient.** Raise extracellular K⁺ and the cell rests less negative (−80, −70 mV)
**High K⁺, first:** K⁺ channels (IKr) conduct better with more K⁺ outside → **faster phase 3** → **tall, narrow, symmetric, tented T with a short QT**; QRS still normal

**High K⁺, second:** partial depolarisation leaves **Na⁺ channels inactivated** → slow phase 0 → **P flattens and disappears** (atria most sensitive; sinoventricular rhythm), **long PR, wide QRS**, bizarre axis, ST elevation in V1–V2 (Brugada phenocopy, pseudo-infarct) → **sine wave** → VF, asystole or PEA
**Same end-point as a Na⁺-channel blocker:** both leave too few working Na⁺ channels, so both widen the QRS
**Low K⁺:** K⁺ channels conduct poorly → **slow phase 3** → flat T, ST depression, **U wave**, long QU → EADs → ectopics, AF, VT, **torsades**; worsens digoxin toxicity
**ECG ≠ potassium meter:** CKD tolerates high levels; a rapid rise, low Ca²⁺ or acidosis makes the same level lethal; the first arrhythmia may be fatal. A normal ECG does not make a high K⁺ safe
**IV calcium** raises the threshold potential, restoring the resting-to-threshold gap: works in **1–3 min, lasts 30–60 min, does not change K⁺**. Given for the ECG change, not the number
new_cards.why: KAL-10 and KAL-06 list the ECG stages with no mechanism. This is the foundation that makes them, the Brugada phenocopy, sinoventricular rhythm and 'calcium does not lower potassium' derivable; also the link QRS = sodium for the poison section.

new_cards.topic: The ICU makers of high potassium, and what each teaches
new_cards.q:
**High potassium in the ICU:**
a Shift out of cells
b Suxamethonium: normal rise, and who arrests
c Reduced excretion and the RTA that raises K⁺
d Pseudohyperkalaemia
e Dialysate K⁺ for emergency dialysis
a: **Shift:** acidosis (mineral > lactic or keto), **insulin lack and hyperosmolality** (DKA: serum K⁺ high but total body K⁺ low: check K⁺ before insulin, replace first if **<3.5 mmol/L**; older ADA 2009 keys: <3.3), rhabdomyolysis, crush, tumour lysis, haemolysis, massive transfusion of old blood, reperfusion, β-blockers, **digoxin overdose** (Na-K ATPase block)

**Suxamethonium:** normal rise about **0.5 mmol/L**. Extrajunctional (immature, α7) receptors after denervation or immobility → rise of **5–10 mmol/L** and arrest: **burns after 24–48 h**, spinal cord injury, stroke, GBS, crush, prolonged ICU immobility
**Excretion:** AKI, CKD, and **low aldosterone effect**: ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, heparin, hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism (diabetic with mild CKD)
**NAGMA + high K⁺ = type 4 RTA.** Types 1 and 2 have a **low** K⁺
**Pseudohyperkalaemia:** haemolysed sample, thrombocytosis, leucocytosis, fist clenching: **normal ECG, well patient** → repeat the sample
**Emergency haemodialysis for K⁺ with ECG change: dialysate K⁺ 1 mmol/L** (keyed). **Not 0** (too rapid a fall is arrhythmogenic); 4–5 removes little; routine baths are 2–3
new_cards.why: GT1 Q36 (missed): NAGMA with hyperkalaemia = type 4 RTA. INI-SS PYT 4 Sep Q33 (missed, cohort 64%): dialysate potassium 1 mEq/L for K⁺ 7.2 with ECG changes. GT1 Q26 (suxamethonium hyperkalaemia). No single card collects the ICU causes.

new_cards.q:
**For the QT interval, give:**
a How to measure it
b Bazett's formula and its fault
c Normal QTc and the danger line
d What to do with a wide QRS
e Short QT: value and causes
a: **QRS onset to T end**, in the lead with the longest QT and a clean T end (usually **II or V5**); **tangent method** (steepest downslope of T to baseline); exclude the U wave

The QT shortens as rate rises, so correct to 60/min: **Bazett QTc = QT ÷ √RR (seconds)**. **Overcorrects at fast rates, undercorrects at slow rates**; Fridericia (cube root) and Framingham (linear) are better at extremes
**Normal QTc ≤450 ms men, ≤460 ms women** (older single limit 440 ms). Quick check at 60–100/min: T ends before half the RR interval
**QTc >500 ms, or a rise >60 ms from baseline = high torsades risk:** stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺
**Wide QRS (BBB, pacing) inflates the QT:** use the **JT interval** or subtract the excess QRS width
**Short QT <340–360 ms:** hypercalcaemia, digoxin, hyperthermia, congenital short QT syndrome
new_cards.why: No card says how the QT is measured or corrected, yet every QT fact (TOX-07, CAR-06, ACLS-16) depends on it. Bazett's over- and under-correction is a standard MCQ.

new_cards.topic: Congenital long QT: three channels, three triggers, and the Schwartz score
new_cards.q:
**Congenital long QT syndrome:**
a LQT1, LQT2, LQT3: gene, current, trigger, T wave
b The two inheritance syndromes
c Schwartz score: the big items and the cut-offs
d Treatment
a: **LQT1: KCNQ1, loss of IKs.** Trigger **exercise, especially swimming**; broad-based T; β-blockers work best
**LQT2: KCNH2 (hERG), loss of IKr.** Trigger **sudden noise (alarm, phone), emotion, postpartum**; low notched T
**LQT3: SCN5A gain of function (late Na⁺ current).** Events at **rest and in sleep**; long flat ST with late peaked T; **mexiletine** helps. (SCN5A loss of function = Brugada)
**Romano-Ward:** autosomal dominant, normal hearing. **Jervell and Lange-Nielsen:** autosomal recessive, sensorineural **deafness**, severe

**Schwartz score:** QTc ≥480 = **3**, 460–479 = 2, 450–459 (men) = 1; QTc ≥480 at 4th min of exercise recovery = 1; torsades = **2**; T-wave alternans = 1; notched T in 3 leads = 1; low rate for age = 0.5; **syncope with stress = 2**, without = 1; congenital deafness = 0.5; relative with definite LQTS = 1; unexplained sudden death <30 in immediate family = 0.5
**≤1 low, 1.5–3 intermediate, ≥3.5 high.** Do not score syncope and torsades together; the same relative cannot earn both family items

Worked: swimmer with syncope (2) + QTc 485 (3) + relative with LQTS (1) + another relative with sudden death <30 (0.5) = **6.5** (GT1 Q3 key). With a family sudden death only and no relative with proven LQTS the strict sum is **5.5**; still high probability
**Treatment:** non-selective β-blocker (**nadolol or propranolol**) for all; avoid QT drugs; keep K⁺ and Mg²⁺ normal; **ICD** after arrest or events on β-blocker; left cardiac sympathetic denervation
new_cards.why: GT1 Q3 (skipped): Schwartz score calculation, keyed 6.5 (high probability). No card holds the score, the genotype triggers or the T-wave shapes.

new_cards.topic: Acquired long QT: the drugs, the states, and the safe choices
new_cards.q:
**Acquired long QT:**
a The shared mechanism
b Drug families
c States that add to the drug
d QTc in organophosphate poisoning: what it means
e Anaesthesia in congenital long QT
a: **Almost all QT drugs block hERG (IKr)**: an acquired LQT2; worse with bradycardia, pauses and low K⁺

**Drugs:** class Ia and III antiarrhythmics; macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azoles, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, quinine; **haloperidol (IV)**, droperidol, ziprasidone, quetiapine, citalopram, TCAs; **ondansetron**, domperidone; methadone; **arsenic trioxide**; volatile anaesthetics
**States:** low K⁺, low Mg²⁺, low Ca²⁺, bradycardia, female sex, structural heart disease, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, liver failure, starvation, SAH and raised ICP, organophosphate poisoning
Several QT drugs together: stop first the one that also inhibits CYP3A4 (erythromycin, fluconazole)
**OP poisoning with a long QTc: 'may indicate increased severity'** (linked to respiratory failure and mortality), but it does not confirm severity or predict atropine resistance

**LQTS anaesthesia: propofol is the safe agent** (no QT prolongation). Volatiles incl. **sevoflurane prolong QTc**; avoid ondansetron, droperidol, ketamine, adrenaline, suxamethonium, neostigmine with anticholinergic; continue the β-blocker; normal K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, temperature; blunt intubation and emergence surges
new_cards.why: GT1 Q147 (missed, cohort 67%): safe anaesthetic in congenital LQTS = propofol. GT8 Q55 (missed): QTc 470 ms in OP poisoning 'may indicate increased severity'. GT7 Q110: arsenic trioxide with QTc prolongation.

new_cards.topic: Sodium-channel blocker toxicity: the TCA pattern and why bicarbonate works
new_cards.q:
**Sodium-channel blocker (tricyclic) poisoning:**
a The ECG pattern and why aVR
b QRS thresholds and what each predicts
c Why bicarbonate works; dose and target
d Drugs never to give
e The threshold in children
f Other drugs with the same picture
a: **Phase 0 block → slow conduction → wide QRS.** The right bundle is hit hardest, so the terminal 40 ms points right and up: **terminal R in aVR ≥3 mm, R/S in aVR >0.7**, deep slurred S in I and aVL; plus sinus tachycardia (anticholinergic), hypotension (α-block), long QT, Brugada-like V1–V2
**QRS ≥100 ms → seizures (about 1 in 3); ≥160 ms → ventricular arrhythmia (about 1 in 2)** (Boehnert and Lovejoy 1985). The QRS, not the dose or the level, grades the risk

**NaHCO₃ works twice:** the sodium load pushes current through unblocked channels; alkalosis reduces drug binding to the channel. **1–2 mmol/kg boluses** for QRS >100 ms, arrhythmia or hypotension, repeated to a narrow QRS; **pH 7.45–7.55**. Hypertonic saline is the alternative

**Never:** class Ia, Ic (more Na⁺ block), class III (QT), **physostigmine** (asystole), **phenytoin** (Na⁺ blocker; seizures get a benzodiazepine). **Lidocaine (Ib)** is the only antiarrhythmic, after bicarbonate
**Children: the same threshold, QRS 100 ms.** A child's normal QRS is narrower, so 100 ms is clearly wide; the aVR R wave is less specific in young children (RV dominance)

**Same picture, same antidote:** cocaine, **propranolol** (membrane-stabilising), flecainide, class Ia, diphenhydramine, carbamazepine, quinine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, lamotrigine, venlafaxine; local anaesthetics (add lipid emulsion)
new_cards.why: GT1 Q139 (skipped): QRS threshold for bicarbonate in a child with TCA overdose = 100 ms. GT7 Q102 (missed): cocaine wide-QRS tachycardia → sodium bicarbonate. GT8 Q52: propranolol QRS 160 ms → bicarbonate. TOX-07 names the drugs but not the aVR sign or why bicarbonate works.

new_cards.topic: Other poisons on the ECG: organophosphates, lithium, antipsychotics, theophylline and the rest
new_cards.q:
**ECG in other poisonings:**
a Organophosphates: the three phases
b Lithium
c Antipsychotics
d Theophylline and caffeine
e Arsenic, carbon monoxide, hydrofluoric acid, loperamide
a: **Organophosphate:** (1) early sinus tachycardia and hypertension (nicotinic); (2) **sinus bradycardia, long PR, AV block** (muscarinic); (3) days later **long QT, ST-T change, polymorphic VT or torsades**. A long QTc **may indicate greater severity** (more respiratory failure and deaths); it does not confirm it
**Lithium:** flat or inverted T (commonest, benign); toxicity → **sinus node dysfunction**, SA block, bradycardia; long QT; unmasks Brugada. Seizures in severe toxicity → **benzodiazepine first**
**Antipsychotics:** long QT (hERG), sinus tachycardia (anticholinergic); thioridazine also widens the QRS

**Theophylline, caffeine** (adenosine antagonism, raised cAMP): sinus tachycardia, **MAT**, SVT, ventricular arrhythmias, hypokalaemia. **Adenosine fails.** SVT → esmolol; ventricular irritability with compromise → amiodarone (GT key); cimetidine raises the level
**Cocaine:** Na⁺ block (wide QRS → bicarbonate), ischaemia and infarction, long QT

**Arsenic trioxide:** long QT, torsades. **Carbon monoxide:** ischaemic ST-T change. **Hydrofluoric acid:** low Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, high K⁺ → long QT, VF. **High-dose loperamide, diphenhydramine:** wide QRS and long QT
new_cards.why: GT8 Q55 (missed): QTc in OP poisoning. GT8 Q73 (missed): seizures in lithium toxicity → benzodiazepines. GT8 Q98: theophylline with ventricular irritability and compromise (keyed amiodarone). GT7 Q110: arsenic trioxide and QTc. TOX-07 lists these drugs only by name.

new_cards.topic: Temperature and hormones on the ECG: hypothermia, thyroid, adrenal, phaeochromocytoma
new_cards.q:
**Temperature and hormones on the ECG:**
a Hypothermia: the sequence
b The Osborn wave: where, why, and its size
c Rough temperature thresholds
d Thyroid: storm and myxoedema
e Adrenal crisis, phaeochromocytoma, raised ICP
a: **Hypothermia:** shivering artefact → **sinus bradycardia** (SA node depressed first) → **slow AF** → **all intervals long (PR, QRS, QT)** → Osborn wave → VF or asystole

**Osborn (J) wave:** positive hump at the J point, best in inferior and V3–V6, negative in aVR; **taller as temperature falls**. Mechanism: the phase 1 (Ito) notch deepens in the epicardium but not the endocardium (same substrate as Brugada)
**Thresholds (approximate):** Osborn wave and AF below **32 °C**; **VF risk below 28 °C** (handle gently); asystole below about 24 °C. Grades and rewarming: V12-035
J wave at normal temperature: **hypercalcaemia**, early repolarisation. Cold blunts the ECG signs of hyperkalaemia

**Thyroid storm, fever:** sinus tachycardia; **AF in 10–25%** of hyperthyroid patients, more in the elderly. **Myxoedema:** sinus bradycardia, **low voltage**, flat T, long QT, AV block, pericardial effusion

**Adrenal crisis:** hyperkalaemic changes (no aldosterone), low voltage. **Phaeochromocytoma:** sinus tachycardia, arrhythmias, catecholamine cardiomyopathy with T inversion and long QT. **Raised ICP:** Cushing bradycardia with hypertension
new_cards.why: V12-035 (Arrest packet) gives the hypothermia sequence without the mechanism or the leads; MI-27 and CAL-10 mention Osborn waves as mimics. Nothing in the decks covers the endocrine ECGs asked as one-liners.
